en: He from whom proceed the birth, etc., of this [universe], who is the knower of all objects through His own connection and disconnection with them, who is self-sovereign—
by Him, the Brahman, was [this] revealed in the heart to the first poet (Brahmā), about whom even the wise are bewildered;
in whom the threefold creation, like the exchange of fire, water, and earth, is not unreal.
We meditate upon the Supreme Truth, whose very nature eternally casts out all deceit. Herein lies the supreme dharma of the virtuous who are free from envy;
here is the reality to be known, which bestows auspiciousness and uproots the threefold suffering.
In this *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam*, composed by the great sage, what need is there for other scriptures?
For those who are skillful and eager to hear, the Lord is immediately captured within the heart at that very moment;
it is the fruit fallen from the celestial wish-fulfilling tree of the Vedas.

O connoisseurs of aesthetic flavor on this earth, O seekers of the divine! Drink again and again the nectar of the *Bhāgavata*, which is blended with the liquid ambrosia from the mouth of Śuka. It is the very abode of rasa. Ah! Drink it repeatedly.

In the Naimiṣa forest, the field of the Unblinking One, the lordly Śaunaka and others were performing a sacrificial session (*satra*) for the sake of the heavenly world, lasting for a thousand years. Once, those sages, having offered oblations into the fires at dawn, [proceeded].
When Sūta had been honored and was seated, the sages respectfully asked him this.
The sages said:
"O sinless one, you have indeed [studied] the Purāṇas along with the Itihāsas."
O Sūta, the Dharmaśāstras that have been recited,
as well as those which the venerable Bādarāyaṇa— the best among the knowers of the Vedas—
and other sages who understand the higher and the lower, know; all these have been studied by me.
"O gentle one, you know all that in its true essence through his grace; for teachers may indeed reveal even the most secret truths to a devoted disciple.
Therefore, O long-lived one, tell us exactly what has been determined by you in each of those matters."
It behoves you to describe that which is the sole and ultimate good for men.
O worthy one, for the most part, the people in this age of Kali are short-lived,
dull-witted, of very feeble intellect, unfortunate, and indeed afflicted by calamities.
There are many scriptures with manifold activities that ought to be heard in their various divisions.
Therefore, O virtuous one, extracting the essence from them here with your wisdom, speak for the welfare of all beings, by which the self becomes perfectly serene.

O Sūta, may you be blessed; you know that the Blessed Lord, the protector of the Sātvatas, was born to Vasudeva through Devakī for the sake of His intended purpose. It behooves You to describe His limbs to us as we long to hear it.
His incarnation is for the welfare and prosperity of all beings;
he who, having fallen into this terrible cycle of worldly existence, chants his name while powerless,
is instantly liberated from it— he who himself fears fear.

O Sūta, those sages who take refuge at his feet and whose very dwelling is tranquility instantly purify those who touch them, just as the waters of the celestial river are purified by their constant service. Who indeed [is capable of describing] that Blessed One, whose deeds are praised in holy verses?
One who desires purity should not fail to hear the glory that removes the impurities of the Kali age.
Tell us, who are full of faith, of his noble deeds celebrated by the wise— deeds performed as he assumed various forms through his divine play.
Now, O wise one, please narrate the auspicious accounts of the incarnations of Hari,
the Lord who freely performs his pastimes through his own *māyā*.
Indeed, we are not satiated by the heroic exploits of the One of Excellent Renown (*uttamaśloka*).

For those who possess the knowledge of aesthetic flavor, Keśava— who, though concealed as a deceptive human, was in truth the Blessed Lord— performed deeds with Rāma that were truly superhuman, each step of which is sweeter than the last for those who hear them.
Knowing that Kali had arrived, we were seated here in this sacred field of Viṣṇu, engaged in a long sacrificial session and eager for discourse on Hari;
you have been shown to us by the Creator to help us cross over what is otherwise difficult to traverse.
Tell me of Kali, which robs men of their essential strength like a helmsman [driving one] into the ocean; and when Kṛṣṇa— the Lord of Yoga, the friend of Brahman, and the armor of Dharma—
has now reached his own ultimate state, to what refuge has Dharma gone?
Vyāsa said:
Thus, the son of Romaharṣaṇa, delighted by the questions of the brahmins,
honored their words and began to speak.
Sūta said:

I bow down to that sage who is the heart of all beings—the one whom Dvaipāyana, distressed by separation, called out as "Son! when he was departing, unaccompanied and having renounced all worldly duties; and at whose name the trees burst into bloom through their absorption in him.

I approach that son of Vyāsa, the teacher of sages, who out of compassion for transmigrating beings desiring to cross the blinding darkness revealed the secret of the Purāṇas— the singular essence of all Vedas, the lamp of the supreme self.
Having offered salutations to Nārāyaṇa and to Nara, the best of men...
One should then invoke the goddess Sarasvatī, Vyāsa, and thereafter Jaya.
O sages, I have been well questioned by you concerning that which is the auspiciousness of the world;
for you have made inquiry about Kṛṣṇa, by whom the self becomes perfectly serene.

That indeed is the supreme dharma for men, from which arises unswerving and unimpeded devotion to Adhokṣaja, by which the self becomes perfectly serene. When the yoga of devotion is practiced toward the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, [it brings about this result].
Dharma well-practiced by men, which consists of stories concerning Viṣvaksena, quickly generates dispassion and knowledge that is independent of any other cause;
if it does not produce delight, it is indeed nothing but mere labor.
For one who seeks liberation, material wealth does not serve the purpose of dharma;
nor is desire intended for the acquisition of wealth that is solely devoted to dharma.
The gratification of the senses is not the goal of desire; rather, one should live with only as much as is necessary for survival.
The desire of the individual soul for the knowledge of reality is not achieved through ritual actions in this world;
those who know reality declare that reality to be non-dual knowledge,
which is designated as Brahman, the Supreme Self, and the Blessed Lord.
The sages, full of faith, perceive the Self within the self through devotion acquired from hearing the scriptures and joined with knowledge and detachment;
therefore, O best of the twice-born, men [should act] according to the divisions of caste and stage of life.
The perfect fulfillment of well-performed dharma is the pleasing of Hari;
therefore, with a single-minded focus, the Blessed Lord, the Master of the Sātvatas,
should always be heard, glorified, meditated upon, and worshipped.

Who would not take delight in the narrations of Him, by meditating upon whom the wise sever the bondage of the knots of karma? For one who is desirous of hearing and full of faith, there arises a relish for the narrations of Vāsudeva.
O brāhmaṇas, by serving the great and by resorting to sacred pilgrimage sites,
Kṛṣṇa— whose hearing and chanting are meritorious— dwells within the hearts of those who listen to His own stories; as the friend of the saintly, He indeed shakes off all misfortunes.
When inauspicious states have almost entirely perished through constant service to the Lord,
unswerving devotion arises toward the Blessed One, the one of exalted fame.
Then, those states of passion and ignorance, as well as desire, greed, and the like, [are destroyed].
When the mind is not pierced by these [qualities] and remains established in goodness (sattva), it becomes serene.
Thus, for one whose mind is serene and who is free from attachment, the realization of the true nature of the Blessed Lord arises through the yoga of devotion to the Blessed Lord.
The knot of the heart is severed, all doubts are cut asunder,
and one's karmas are exhausted upon seeing the Lord, the Self, even here and now.
Therefore, the wise always cultivate devotion with supreme joy.
In Vāsudeva, the Blessed One, they perform that which brings tranquility to the self.

Sattva, rajas, and tamas are the qualities of *prakṛti*; endowed with these, the one Supreme Person assumes here in this world the names Hari, Viriñci, and Hara for the sake of the maintenance and other functions of this universe. Among those names, indeed, the auspicious benefits for men accrue from Him whose body is composed of *sattva*.
From earth comes smoke, from that fire consisting of the three Vedas;
from darkness (tamas) comes passion (rajas), and from that comes goodness (sattva), which is the vision of Brahman. Then, in the beginning, the sages took refuge in the Blessed One Adhokṣaja.
Those who follow after that pure *sattva* become fit for security in this world; then,
desiring liberation, those free from envy abandon the fierce-formed lords of beings and worship the peaceful portions of Nārāyaṇa.

Those whose natures are characterized by *rajas* and *tamas*, possessing similar dispositions and desiring prosperity, power, and progeny, indeed worship the Pitṛs, the Bhūtas, the Prajeśas, and others.
The Vedas have Vāsudeva as their ultimate goal; the sacrifices have Vāsudeva as their ultimate goal.
Yoga has Vāsudeva as its supreme goal; ritual actions have Vāsudeva as their supreme goal.
Knowledge has Vāsudeva as its supreme goal; austerity has Vāsudeva as its supreme goal.
Dharma has Vāsudeva as its supreme goal; the ultimate destination has Vāsudeva as its supreme goal.

In the beginning, that very Lord, the omnipresent one who is beyond the modes of nature, created this universe by means of His own creative power (*māyā*), which consists of the modes of nature and takes the form of both the manifest and the unmanifest.
Amidst these qualities manifested by that power, He appears as if He Himself possessed those qualities.
Having entered within, He shines forth, manifested through consciousness;
for just as fire, though one, when placed within its own source— the pieces of wood—
appears as if manifold, so too does the Supreme Person, the Soul of the universe, appear diverse among all beings.

Entering into beings through the states composed of the modes— consisting of the subtle elements, the senses, and the ego— he experiences those qualities within the beings he himself has created. As the creator of the worlds, he indeed sustains the worlds through the mode of goodness (*sattva*).
Delighting in his pastimes and incarnations among gods, animals, humans, and others—
Sūta said:
"The Blessed One assumed a human form through the great elements and other principles."

In the beginning, for the desire to emit the worlds, He brought forth that which consists of sixteen parts; from the lotus in the lake of the navel of Him who was lying upon the waters, spreading His yogic sleep, there arose Brahmā, the lord of the creators of the universe.
The expansion of the worlds is fashioned from the arrangement of His limbs;
that indeed is the form of the Blessed One, pure and powerful *sattva*.
They behold that wondrous form—possessing a thousand feet, thighs, arms, and faces—with their vast vision.
With a thousand heads, ears, eyes, and noses, and resplendent with a thousand crowns, garments, and earrings—
this is the imperishable seed and the repository of all various incarnations,
by a minute fraction of whose parts gods, animals, humans, and others are created.
That very same Lord, having first undertaken the Kaumāra creation,
practiced the difficult-to-perform, unbroken vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) as Brahmā. Then, for the sake of his manifestation, he [raised] the earth that had gone to the netherworld (*rasātala*).
Intending to uplift [the world], the Lord of Sacrifice assumed the body of a boar;
and having attained the status of a celestial sage during the third creation of the sages,
He taught the Sātvata-tantra, through which the cessation of karmic bondage is achieved by means of action.
In the fourth creation, that of the portions of dharma, he became the two sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa and performed difficult austerities endowed with self-serenity.
In the fifth, he became the lord of the perfected ones named Kapila, who [revealed] that which had been obscured by time.
He taught Sāṅkhya, which determines the collection of principles, to Asuri;
and having been chosen by Anasūyā as the sixth son of Atri, he attained that status.
He spoke on Ānvīkṣikī to Alarka and others, such as Prahlāda.
Then, in the seventh [manvantara], Yajña was born from Ruci through Ākūti;
he protected the period of Svāyambhuva along with the hosts of gods beginning with Yāma.
In the eighth [manvantara], however, Urukrama was born to Nābhi through Merudevī.
Displaying the path of the wise, which is honored by all stages of life,
he assumed a ninth earthly form at the request of the sages; by him,
the Brahmins milked these medicinal herbs from this earth, and therefore he is most beloved.
During the dissolution of the waters of Cākṣuṣa Manu's ocean, He assumed the form of a fish; having placed Vaivasvata Manu upon a boat made of earth,
He protected him while the gods and demons were churning the ocean with Mount Mandara as the churning-stick.
In his eleventh incarnation, the omnipresent Lord assumed the form of a tortoise and supported [the mountain] upon his back. In the twelfth, he appeared as Dhanvantari, and in the thirteenth,
he beguiled the gods with the woman Mohinī, while causing them to drink the nectar.
In His fourteenth incarnation as Nṛsiṃha, assuming a form of great power, He tore open the chest of the mighty lord of the Daityas with His claws,
just as a cat tears open a rat.
In His fifteenth incarnation, having assumed the form of Vāmana, He went to the sacrifice of Bali.
Begging for three paces of land while desiring to take back the triple heaven, and seeing kings who were enemies of the Brahmanas during his sixteenth incarnation,
he became enraged and thrice seven times rendered the earth devoid of Kshatriyas.
Then, in the seventeenth [generation], he was born to Satyavatī from Parāśara;
seeing that men were of small intelligence, he divided the branches of the tree of the Veda.
Having attained the state of a god among men, he acted out of a desire to accomplish the work of the gods.

After this, in the nineteenth and twentieth chapters, the Blessed One performed such heroic deeds as the subduing of the ocean; having taken birth among the Vṛṣṇis as Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, he removed the burden of the earth.
Then, when the Kali age has fully set in, for the purpose of deluding the enemies of the gods,
he will appear among the Kīkaṭas under the name of Buddha, the son of Añjana. Furthermore, at the junction of the ages, while kings consist mostly of bandits, he will appear.
The progenitor of Viṣṇuyaśas shall be named Kalki, the Lord of the World. O twice-born ones, the incarnations of Hari, the treasury of goodness, are indeed innumerable,
just as thousands of small streams may flow from a single lake.
The sages, the Manus, the gods, and the sons of Manu of great prowess— all these,
along with the Prajāpatis, are known to be but portions (kalās) of Hari alone.
These are indeed partial manifestations (aṃśakalās) of the Supreme Person, but Kṛṣṇa is the Lord himself.

Those men who, being self-controlled, recite with devotion morning and evening this secret birth of the Blessed One— which in every age brings relief to the world distressed by the enemies of Indra— are liberated from the multitude of sufferings.
This form of the Blessed One, who is indeed formless and whose nature is consciousness,
has been fashioned within Himself by the qualities of Māyā through the principles beginning with Mahat,
just as a mass of clouds appears in the sky or dust in the wind.
Thus, the state of being an object of vision has been superimposed upon the Seer by those lacking intelligence.
Beyond this is that which is unmanifest (*avyakta*), not augmented by the expansion of the *guṇas*;
because its nature is neither seen nor heard, it is the individual soul (*jīva*), which undergoes rebirth.
When both existence and non-existence, which are superimposed upon the Self by ignorance, are negated through self-realization— that is the vision of Brahman;
provided that this divine Māyā has ceased and the intellect has attained the state of pure discernment.
They know him to be already perfect; he is magnified in his own glory.
Thus do the sages describe the births and activities of the Lord of the heart—the Unborn and the Non-doer—as secrets of the Vedas.
He, whose pastimes are never in vain, creates this entire universe, protects it, and devours it; yet He is not attached to it.
Hidden within all beings, independent by His own nature, and the Lord of the six divine qualities, He experiences the objects of the six senses.
No living being, however clever, can understand the ways of that Creator, for they are beyond the reach of the dull-witted.
He who, like an ignorant man performing the role of an actor, extends through his mind and speech the names and forms [of the Lord],
knows the path of the Supreme Creator, whose prowess is boundless and whose hand holds the discus;
he who, with unceasing and guileless devotion, worships the fragrance of His lotus feet.

But here on earth, those blessed ones are truly fortunate who thus direct their entire being toward Vāsudeva, the Lord of all worlds and the Self of all, wherein there is no further fierce cycle of rebirth.
This is the Purāṇa named Bhāgavata, which is equal to the Veda.
The blessed sage composed this account of the deeds of Uttamaśloka for the ultimate welfare of the world— a work that is auspicious, a great means of securing well-being— and he caused his son,
the best among those who possess self-mastery, to master it.
Having extracted the very essence of all the Vedas and Itihāsas,
he recited it to the great king Parīkṣit,
who was seated in the vow of fasting on the Gaṅgā and surrounded by supreme sages.
When Kṛṣṇa had returned to His own abode along with dharma, knowledge, and the other perfections,
this sun of the Purāṇas has now risen for those whose vision is lost in the Kali age.
O brahmins, while that sage among brahmins of immense splendor was thus proclaiming it, [the gods arrived].
"And I, having settled there, attained [this knowledge] through his grace;
therefore, I shall cause you to hear it exactly as I have studied it and according to my understanding.
Vyāsa said:
Having thus praised Sūta as he was speaking, the aged Kulapati Śaunaka, a master of the Ṛgveda, addressed him while the sages were performing a long sacrificial session. Śaunaka said:

O Sūta, O Sūta, O highly fortunate one, best among speakers, tell us the meritorious narrative of the Lord (Bhāgavata) which the blessed Śuka related. In which age did this [narrative] begin, in what place, and for what reason?
Impelled by whom did the sage Kṛṣṇa compose this *Saṃhitā*?
His son was a great yogi, impartial and free from conceptual construction; with his mind fixed on the One, ever-awake, he remained hidden like one who is dull-witted.
Seeing that his son, the sage, was following him even though he was naked, the queens, out of shame, did not clothe their son;

yet, seeing this, when the sage questioned them, they replied: "O you of discerning vision, for you there is no distinction between male and female, but for your son there is. How was he recognized by the citizens upon his arrival in Kurujāṅgala?

O dear one, how did this conversation between the royal sage of the Pāṇḍavas and the sage take place in Hastināpura— wherein this Sātvata revelation was revealed— while he was wandering about like one who is mad, mute, or dull-witted?
O Sūta, that illustrious one, making his very hermitage a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), looked upon even the time it takes for householders to milk their cows in their homes;
him they call the son of Abhimanyu, the supreme devotee of the Lord (*bhāgavatottama*).
Relate to us his most wonderful birth and his deeds;
for what reason did that sovereign, the enhancer of the Pāṇḍus,
disregard royal splendor and sit in a vow of fasting upon the Gaṅgā?
Even enemies abandon their wealth to bow down at the abode of his feet for the sake of their own welfare;

O dear one, how could that hero, while still young, wish to cast away prosperity so difficult to relinquish, even along with his very life? Those people who are devoted to the Lord of Excellent Renown (Uttamaśloka) act for the peace, existence, and prosperity of the world.
"Living beings do not exist for their own sake; why then did he, having become disillusioned with this dependence on another, cast off his body?
Tell us all that, since we have asked you about it here.
I consider you to be one who has bathed in the waters of speech, except perhaps for those who are experts in the Vedic hymns."
Sūta said:
When the third cycle of the Yugas had arrived, namely the Dvāpara age,
the yogi Parāśara was born of Vāsavyā as a portion of Hari.
Once, having sipped the pure water of the Sarasvatī,
that sage— knowing both the higher and the lower— who was alone in a secluded place, sat down as the orb of the sun had risen; he was thus situated by Time, whose speed is unmanifest.
In age after age, he perceives the corruption of the dharma of the ages occurring upon the earth,
as well as the decline in the power of material beings caused thereby;
[he sees those who] lack faith, are devoid of strength, are dull-witted, and have diminished lifespans.

Beholding with his divine eye those people who were unfortunate, the sage of unfailing vision meditated upon what would be beneficial for all the social orders (*varṇas*) and stages of life (*āśramas*). He then beheld the pure Vedic ritual of the four officiating priests (*cāturhotra*) intended for the progeny.
For the continuity of sacrifice, he divided the single Veda into fourfold form.
The four Vedas known as Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharvan were extracted;
and the Itihāsa-Purāṇa is called the fifth Veda.
Among them, Paila was the upholder of the Ṛgveda, the wise Jaimini was the singer of the Sāman,
Vaiśampāyana alone was proficient in the Yajus,
and the austere sage Sumantu was the master of the Atharvāṅgirasa.
My father Romaharṣaṇa was the author of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.
These sages, having divided their respective Vedas in many ways, transmitted them through disciples, grand-disciples, and their disciples; thus the Vedas came to have many branches.
Just as those very Vedas are maintained by men of dull intellect,
even so did the Blessed Vyāsa, who is compassionate toward the wretched, act;
for the Triple Veda (Trayī) was not within the range of hearing for women, Śūdras, and the low-born among the twice-born.
"May the welfare of those deluded regarding the highest good through ritual action be thus attained here"—
with this thought, the sage composed the narrative of the *Bhārata* out of compassion.
O twice-born ones, he was thus always engaged in promoting the welfare of all beings.
When his heart was not satisfied even by that which consists of all things,
and his heart remained somewhat dissatisfied, he— knowing the dharma, staying alone in a pure place on the bank of the Sarasvatī, and reflecting— spoke this.
For by me, who am firm in my vows and free from guile, the Vedas, the teachers, and the sacred fires have been honored, and their instruction has been received; and indeed,
the meaning of the Vedas has been revealed under the designation of the *Bhārata*.
In this [scripture], even women, śūdras, and others perceive dharma and other goals;
nevertheless, alas, my own self, though all-pervading, appears as if incomplete to me, even though I am the best among those endowed with the splendor of Brahman.
Or rather, have the duties of the devotees (*bhāgavata-dharma*) not been described for the most part?
For those very duties are dear to the *paramahaṃsas*, and they alone are dear to Acyuta.
To him, who thus considered himself deficient and was distressed...

Nārada came to the hermitage previously described, which belonged to Kṛṣṇa. Recognizing that he had arrived, the sage immediately rose to greet him and honored Nārada, who is worshipped by the gods, according to the prescribed rites.
Sūta said: Then,
as he sat comfortably nearby,
the celestial sage of great renown, lute in hand, spoke to the brahmin sage as if smiling.
Nārada said:
O highly fortunate son of Parāśara, is your physical self or even your mental self satisfied with yourself?
Your desire has been perfectly fulfilled by you, who have composed the most wonderful *Bhārata*, which is enriched with all meaningful subjects;
and that eternal Brahman which was sought after has been studied.
"Nevertheless, O Lord, you grieve for yourself as if your purpose were unfulfilled.
Vyāsa said:
"All this that you have spoken is indeed true for me; nevertheless, my soul is not fully satisfied."
We inquire of You, the root of that [unmanifest], whose consciousness is unfathomable, who are the self-born source of the Self;

for You indeed know all secrets, as the ancient Puruṣa who has been worshipped. The Lord of the high and the low creates, protects, and devours the universe by His very mind, remaining unattached through the modes of nature.
"You wander through the three worlds like the sun, moving within them like the wind, the witness of the self;
please examine thoroughly whatever deficiency there may be in me, who have been purified by my vows and righteous conduct regarding the higher and lower Brahman.
Śrī Nārada said:
O venerable one, the stainless glory of the Blessed One has been narrated by you almost in its entirety;
yet I consider that vision alone to be incomplete, for it is that which He Himself would not be satisfied with.
Just as the goals of life, beginning with dharma, have been proclaimed by the best of sages, [so too is His glory].
The majesty of Vāsudeva has not been described in such a manner;
nor has His speech ever been heard, which, with its wonderful words, proclaims the glory of Hari that purifies the world.
Those whose minds are set on Him declare that any place where such speech does not exist is a crow’s watering-hole, for there the swans do not dwell, longing for the nectar of His praise.

The utterance of his speech is a flood that washes away the sins of the people; for even when it is not composed verse by verse, the virtuous hear, sing, and praise the names of the Infinite, which are marked with his glory.
Even the stainless knowledge of liberation, if devoid of devotion to Acyuta, does not shine, however sufficient it may be.
Furthermore, from where could there ever come eternal misfortune for one who has not offered his actions— even those performed without motive— to the Lord?
Moreover, O illustrious one, you whose vision is unfailing, whose fame is pure, who delight in truth and are firm in your vows,
meditate with concentration upon the deeds of the Wide-striding One (Urukrama) for the sake of liberation from all bonds.

Therefore, for one who desires to speak otherwise than this, the intellect— which perceives things as separate and is conditioned by the forms and names [of such views]— will never find a firm footing anywhere, like a boat struck by the wind. For one who instructs others in dharma while being personally attached to his own nature, there is a great transgression.
Or rather, people do not consider it a matter of dharma according to his word, nor do they accept the prevention of that which others have established.
A wise person ought to understand that the happiness of the all-pervading Lord, who is infinite and boundless, arises from cessation;
whereas for one who is not the Self, happiness proceeds through the modes of nature. Therefore, O Lord, please demonstrate the activity of the All-pervading One.

If one who is immature abandons his own duty (*svadharma*) and, while worshiping the lotus feet of Hari, should nevertheless fall from that state, what misfortune has befallen him, or what purpose has been gained by those who worship according to their own duty?
For that very reason, the wise person should strive; for that which is not obtained even by those wandering above and below [in the worlds] cannot be attained otherwise.
That happiness which is obtained elsewhere is like misery; with the passage of time, whose flow is everywhere profound, it eventually fades.
O dear one, a person who serves Mukunda never wanders through the cycle of birth and death in any way whatsoever, like others do.
A person who relishes the aesthetic flavor of the Lord will not wish to abandon again the embrace of Mukunda’s feet, even while remembering them.
For this entire universe is like the Blessed Lord and nothing else, since from Him come the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world;

You indeed know that Yourself, yet You have shown to us only a small portion of Your being. O You of unfailing vision, perceive Yourself as the Self—the portion of the Supreme Person, the Supreme Soul.
Let this manifestation of the Unborn for the welfare of the world be recognized as the supreme exaltation of His great majesty. For this—

namely, the description of the qualities of the One of Excellent Renown— is determined by the wise to be the unfailing fruit of a man’s austerity, sacred learning, well-performed sacrifice, eloquent hymns, and the gifts bestowed with intelligence.

O Sage, in a past life, I was the son of a certain maidservant of those who recite the Vedas. Even as a young boy, I was appointed by the yogis to serve them as they were about to enter their retreat during the rainy season. While I was free from all fickleness, self-controlled, without toys, and obedient to them, [they became pleased].

Although the sages, who perceive all equally, showed compassion toward me as I served them while speaking little, I ate once those remnants of their food with the approval of the twice-born; thus, my sins were cast away.
For one who acts in this way with a purified mind, a natural delight in that very dharma arises within the self.
There, day after day, I heard the enchanting stories of Kṛṣṇa being sung by those who were singing them out of grace for me.
O dear one, as I listened to those stories of Him whose fame is beloved with increasing faith, my inclination toward Him grew.
O great-minded one, at that time, my mind became unwaveringly fixed upon Him whose fame is beloved, now that I had gained such an inclination.
By which [power] I perceive this world of being and non-being, fashioned within Me, the Supreme Brahman, through My own Māyā; thus,

as I constantly heard the pure glory of Hari being proclaimed by high-souled sages during the seasons of autumn and the rainy season, devotion arose, dispelling the passion and darkness of my own nature.
To me— who am thus devoted, humble, cleansed of sin, full of faith, childlike, self-controlled, and a follower— He,
the Blessed Lord Himself, has declared that which is the most secret knowledge.
As they were about to depart, those who are compassionate toward the distressed spoke out of pity:
"By that very means by which I have come to know the power of the illusory energy (*māyā*) of the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, the Creator— by that same means others go to His abode."

O Brahmin, this has been indicated as the remedy for the threefold suffering: that one's action (karma) is performed with devotion toward the Lord, the Blessed One, who is Brahman. And whatever disease arises among living beings, O observer of noble vows, by which [it is cured]—[this too has been shown].
For indeed, that very substance which is diseased does not purify itself even when treated by medicine;

likewise, all ritual practices (*kriyā-yoga*) for men are causes of worldly existence (*saṃsṛti*). When these same practices are conceived as being directed toward the Supreme, they lead to the destruction of the self.
Whatever action is performed here that gratifies the Blessed Lord,
and whatever knowledge there is, is indeed dependent upon Him and endowed with the yoga of devotion;
for they perform their actions there repeatedly according to the instruction of the Blessed Lord.
They chant the qualities and names of Kṛṣṇa and remember them, saying:
"Oṃ, we meditate upon You, the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva;
obeisances to Pradyumna, Aniruddha, and Saṅkarṣaṇa."

Thus, by means of the designation of the forms, that man who possesses perfect vision worships the Lord of Sacrifice— who is both with form as the mantra-form and without form— O Brahmin, having understood this, my own scripture, which was established by me.
Keśava bestowed upon me knowledge, sovereignty, and devotion toward Himself.
You too, O one of vast learning, have heard of that which, when fully realized, satisfies the desire for knowledge of the wise.
Please describe how those whose souls are repeatedly tormented by sufferings may find the extinction of their afflictions; they do not seek it otherwise.
Sūta said:
O Brahmin, having thus heard of the birth and deeds of the divine sage (Nārada),
Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, questioned him further.
Vyāsa said:
When you had been left alone by the mendicants who were your instructors in spiritual knowledge,
what did you do, O Lord, during that first stage of life?

O son of Svāyambhuva, by what means did you spend your later years? And how did you cast off this body when the time had come? O best of sages, you possess this memory of the events of the previous kalpa.
"For this time is indeed an obstacle; it is the destroyer of everything.
Nārada said:
"When I was left alone by the mendicants who were my instructors in spiritual knowledge,"
While I was still in my childhood years, I did this: I had an only daughter, a young woman who was foolish and a slave;
out of affection for her, she bound herself with ties of love toward me, her son, who had no other refuge.

Desiring my welfare, she was not independent and could not provide for her own security; for the world is under the control of the Lord, like a wooden puppet. And I too lived in that family of brahmins out of indifference toward her.
A five-year-old boy, unacquainted with the directions, places, or times,
once saw a cow grazing on the path at night after it had left the house;
impelled by Time, a serpent, touched by his foot, bit the poor creature.
Then, regarding that as a favor from the Lord who desires the welfare of His devotees, I set out toward the northern direction,
where there were flourishing provinces containing cities, villages, cow-pens, and mines.
He saw villages, hamlets, and gardens, as well as forests and groves;
mountains variegated with diverse minerals, where trees were broken by the trunks of elephants;
and reservoirs of auspicious water, lotus ponds frequented by the gods.

I alone passed through that vast forest, which was filled with birds of diverse calls and shimmering with the beauty of wandering bees, and which was dense with thickets of *nalas*, bamboos, reeds, *kuśa* grass, and *kīcaka* canes.
In that place, which was formidable and terrifying in appearance, with its courtyard filled with wandering owls and jackals, my senses and mind were utterly exhausted; overcome by thirst and hunger,
I bathed in a lake of the river, drank, and having sipped the water, my fatigue departed.
In that uninhabited forest, seated upon the seat of a *pippala* tree,
I meditated with my mind conquered by devotion upon the Self abiding within the self, according to what I had heard, while contemplating His lotus feet.

O sage, as my eyes were filled with streams of tears from longing, Hari gradually appeared within my heart; my limbs bristled with horripilation as I was overwhelmed by the weight of love, and being utterly blissful and immersed in a flood of joy, I could perceive neither of the two.
Not seeing that form of the Blessed One— which is so dear to the mind and dispels all sorrow— he suddenly rose up, as if dejected with distress,
desiring to behold it once more by fixing his mind within his heart.
Even while looking, I did not see [Him], as if I were a sick man unsatiated; thus,
as I was striving in that solitary place, the one who is beyond the range of words spoke to me in a voice that was deep and smooth, as if to soothe my grief.
"Alas! In this birth, you ought not to look upon me here.
I am difficult to perceive for those of immature passions and for practitioners of flawed yoga.
O sinless one, this form which has been shown to you once was for the sake of your desire."
One who desires Me gradually abandons all the afflictions dwelling in the heart;
through long service to the saintly, a firm conviction in Me arises,
and having left this flawed world, you shall become one of My people.

"May this intellect of mine remain fixed upon Me and never fail, even during the dissolution of created beings; and by My grace, may my memory [of this] endure. Having said this much, that Great Being, the Lord who is signless yet characterized by the sky, became silent.
And I, moved by compassion, bowed my head in reverence to that most exalted among the great;
with shame cast aside, I recited the secret, auspicious, and glorious names of the Infinite One and remembered His deeds,
wandering the earth with a contented mind, free from longing, devoid of pride and envy, awaiting the end of time.
O Brahmin, while Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana was thus absorbed in thought, his mind unattached and his soul stainless,
time manifested itself like a flash of lightning in the sky at the proper moment,
even as he was applying himself to that pure, divine body of mine.
When his prārabdha-karma was exhausted, that body composed of the five elements fell; then,
at the end of the kalpa, as the Lord desired to sleep upon the waters of the ocean, taking this universe with Him, I entered His breath as He lay down.
At the end of a thousand yugas, as He arose desiring to create this universe,
the sages headed by Marīci and I were born from His vital breaths. With my vows unimpaired, I wander through the three worlds, both within and without.
By the grace of Mahāviṣṇu, I encounter no obstacles anywhere;
having tuned this lute, Devadattā, which is adorned with the sacred sound of the notes,
I wander about singing the stories of Hari.
As he sings of his own heroic deeds, Tīrthapāda Priyaśravas approaches my mind for a swift vision, as if summoned by me;
for this is the state of those whose minds are afflicted by the repeated desire for the touch of sense objects.
The description of Hari’s activities is seen as a boat for crossing the ocean of worldly existence; yet,
for one repeatedly struck by desire and greed, the self is not truly pacified through the paths of yoga such as *yama* and the like in the same way that it is through service to Mukunda.
"O sinless one, all this that I was asked by you— the secret of my births and deeds, which brings satisfaction to your soul— has been narrated. Sūta said:

Having spoken thus to the son of Vasavi, the blessed sage Nārada, who wanders at will, took leave of him and departed while playing his lute. [The people thought: "Oh, how fortunate is this celestial sage, that he sings the glory of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow!"
Singing and rejoicing, he delights this afflicted world with his lute.
Śaunaka said:
O Sūta, when Nārada had departed, the venerable Bādarāyaṇa—
Having heard what was intended by him, what did the omnipresent Lord do next?
Sūta said:
On the western bank of the Sarasvatī river, the river of Brahmā, there is a hermitage.
It is said that the place called Śamyāprāsa increases the merit of the sages' sacrificial sessions.
There, in his own hermitage adorned with groves of jujube trees, Vyāsa sat down,
touched water for purification, and composed his mind in meditation.
When the mind was properly fixed upon the stainless [Self] through the yoga of devotion,
he beheld the Perfect Person and the Māyā that rests upon Him; by which Māyā the individual soul (jīva) is deluded, perceiving itself as consisting of the three guṇas.
Even though others consider it to be useless and encounter the misfortunes caused by it,
the wise sage composed the *Sātvata-saṃhitā* for the sake of the world that does not understand— directly for the sake of the cessation of misfortune through the yoga of devotion to Adhokṣaja.
When this [Saṃhitā] is heard concerning Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person,
devotion arises in a person that removes grief, delusion, and fear;
having thus composed this Bhāgavata Saṃhitā and transmitted it to his son, he [entrusted it to him].
The sage taught Śuka, who was devoted to renunciation.
Śaunaka said:
"How indeed did that sage, who was devoted to renunciation and indifferent toward everything,"
"Or who, delighting in the Self, would practice this great [Bhagavatī]?
Sūta said:
"Even the sages who delight in the Self and are free from all bonds [sought refuge] in the one of vast strides (Urukrama)."
Lord Hari possesses such qualities that He inspires causeless devotion in those who practice it;
and the venerable son of Bādarāyaṇa, whose mind was captivated by the qualities of Hari and who was eternally dear to the devotees of Viṣṇu, studied this great narrative.
I shall now describe the birth and deeds of the royal sage Parīkṣit, which dispel worldly delusion, as well as the passing away of the sons of Pāṇḍu and the unfolding of the stories of Kṛṣṇa;
[this occurred] when, in the battle between the Kauravas and Sṛñjayas, the heroes had attained the destination of heroes.
When the thigh-staffs of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son were shattered by the impact of the mace hurled by Vṛkodara, Aśvatthāman,
seeing it as a service to his master, offered the heads of the sleeping sons of Kṛṣṇā;
people condemn that loathsome deed as being truly disagreeable to him.
Hearing of the terrible death of her sons, the mother was consumed by grief and wept, her eyes clouded with tears. Then the one adorned with a crown and garland, consoling her, said:
"O blessed lady, I shall wipe away your sorrow; for I shall take the head of that wretched Brahmin, that murderous assailant."
"O you whose sons have been burnt, I shall bring [your son] here so that, having attacked him with arrows released from the *gāṇḍīva*, you may bathe [in his blood].
Having thus consoled his beloved wife with charming and varied words, the charioteer of Acyuta’s friend,
clad in armor and wielding a formidable bow, pursued the preceptor’s son on his chariot, which bore the banner of the monkey.
Seeing him rushing toward him from afar, the boy, his mind agitated, fled in his chariot across the earth,

seeking to save his life, as far as he could go out of fear of Rudra, like anyone else in such a plight. When he saw that his horses were exhausted and he had no refuge, he looked about for protection.
The son of the twice-born considered the Brahmaśiras weapon to be his means of self-protection;
then, having sipped water, he composed himself and discharged it,
even though he was unaware that the time for its withdrawal had arrived and his life was in peril.
Then, beholding that fierce radiance manifested in every direction—
a source of peril to his life— the victorious Arjuna spoke to Viṣṇu. Arjuna said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, O mighty-armed one, bestower of fearlessness upon Your devotees!
You alone are the liberation for those being scorched by the cycle of worldly existence.
You are the primordial Puruṣa, the manifest Lord, beyond material nature."
Having cast aside *māyā* by means of Your conscious power (*cicchakti*), You abide in the absolute Self (*kaivalya*). Yet, for the world of living beings whose minds are deluded by *māyā*,
You ordain their welfare through Your own potency in the form of dharma and other virtues.
Likewise, this incarnation of Yours is for the purpose of removing the burden of the earth and for the repeated contemplation of Your own devotees who possess undivided devotion.
O God of gods, I do not know what this is or from whence it comes.
A most terrible radiance comes forth from every direction.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Do you recognize this Brahma-weapon displayed by the son of Droṇa?"
When his life was threatened, he did not know how to withdraw that weapon;
for he possessed no other weapon capable of countering it.
"O knower of weapons, withdraw the fierce energy of your weapon by means of the power of your own weapon! [he said.]
Sūta said: Having heard what was spoken by the Blessed One, Phālguna, the slayer of enemy heroes,
touched water, circumambulated him, and aimed the Brahma-weapon.

Having combined their respective splendors, which were contained within the arrows, they increased like the sun and fire, enveloping the two worlds and the intermediate space. Beholding the great power of those two weapons, which was burning the three worlds, [he saw it]...
As all the creatures were being consumed by fire, they perceived it as the *saṃvartaka* (the fire of universal destruction); observing this affliction of the people and that upheaval of the world,
Arjuna withdrew both [the bow and the arrow] at the command of Vāsudeva.
Then, having swiftly approached the fierce son of Gautamī,
his eyes copper-red with indignation, he bound him like an animal with a rope;
having forcibly bound his enemy with a cord, he desired to lead him away to Śibi.
The lotus-eyed Lord, becoming enraged, said to Arjuna:
"O Pārtha, you ought not to protect this wretched Brahmin; slay him, for he killed sleeping children at night while they were innocent."

One who knows the dharma does not strike an enemy who is intoxicated, heedless, insane, asleep, a child, a woman, an idiot, one who has sought refuge, one deprived of his chariot, or one who is terrified. That pitiless villain who nourishes his own life at the expense of the lives of others is a wicked man.
Indeed, his death would be for his own welfare, since it is because of his fault that a man falls to a lower state;
and you have promised me, while I was listening,
O proud lady, that you would bring back the head of him who has slain your son.
"Therefore, let this wicked man be put to death; he is an assassin who has slain his own kinsman, O hero, and that disgrace to his lineage has done what is displeasing to his master.
Sūta said:

Thus, while examining the matter of dharma, the great son of Pṛthā, urged by Kṛṣṇa, did not wish to kill the son of his guru, even though he had slain his own father. Then, having returned to his own camp, the beloved charioteer of Govinda—
He reported to his grieving beloved that their sons had been killed;

likewise, he described how the teacher’s son had been seized like an animal, bound with ropes, and cast face-down by one loathsome for his deeds. Beholding this injury done to her husband by Kṛṣṇa, she, being of a contrary nature, bowed down out of compassion.
And Satī, unable to endure his being bound and led away, said: "Let him be released, let this Brāhmaṇa be released— he who is a most venerable teacher,
possessing the entire science of archery along with its secret doctrines, including both its discharge and its withdrawal."
And it was by his grace that you were instructed in the entire collection of weapons;
that very Lord Droṇa exists here in the form of a progenitor. Half of his self is his wife, Kṛpī, the mother of heroes, who did not follow him [to death].

O knower of dharma, O highly fortunate one, your family is worthy of honor and should not incur sin, for it is constantly to be revered and saluted. Let Gautamī, his mother and devoted to her husband, not weep.
Just as I, pained by the death of my child, weep repeatedly with a tearful face, so too does that lineage—
along with its followers— burn with grief when the family of the Brahmins has been provoked to anger by kings who have not conquered themselves.
Sūta said:
O twice-born ones, King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, joyfully welcomed the words of the queen, which were righteous, logical, compassionate, sincere, impartial, and sublime.
Nakula, Sahadeva, Yuyudhāna, Dhanañjaya,
the Blessed Lord who is the son of Devakī, and whoever else [was present], as well as the women— thereupon Bhīma spoke in indignation: "The slaying of that man is considered the best course."

Having heard the words spoken by Bhīma and Draupadī—that he had pointlessly killed sleeping children for neither the sake of his master nor his own—and having looked at the face of his friend, the four-armed Lord spoke these words as if smiling: bhagavānuvāca na hyasya durmaterbrahman kāmam prāpsyati durmatim / yo 'yam maddarśanād eva muktaḥ syāc chāpato hareḥ // yathāham bhagavataḥ sākṣāt kṛṣṇasya paramātmanaḥ / draṣṭā dṛṣṭo 'si me tadvat saṅkarṣaṇasahāyavān // tasmān mucyeta śāpāddhi hareḥ sa brahmakopajaḥ / maddarśanāt tvayā prokto yasmān mucyeta kilbiṣāt // iti śrīmadbhāgavate mahāpurāṇe pāramahaṃsyāṃ saṃhitāyāṃ prathamaskandhe śrīkapiladevatīrthayātrāyāṃ śukotpattirnāma saptamo 'dhyāyaḥ // The Blessed Lord said: "O brāhmaṇa, this evil-minded man shall not obtain his wicked desire; for simply by the sight of Me, he is released from the curse of Hari. Just as you have seen Me directly, O Supreme Soul Kṛṣṇa, together with Saṅkarṣaṇa, so too has he been seen by Me. Therefore, he shall indeed be freed from the curse born of Brahmā's anger; because he was told by you to be released from his sin upon seeing Me. Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Birth of Śuka," in the first book of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa, the Pāramahaṃsya Saṃhitā, concerning the pilgrimage of the divine Kapila.
The Blessed Lord said:
"A mere nominal Brahmin must not be killed, even if he is an assailant deserving of death; both these rules have been ordained by me alone—protect them as my instruction."
"Make true your promise which you gave while consoling your beloved—
the promise that was pleasing to Bhīmasena, to the princess of Pañcāla, and to me as well.
Sūta said:
Arjuna, suddenly understanding the intention of Hari,
then seized with his sword the jewel from the head of the brahmin, along with the hair upon it— the jewel which had lost its luster due to the murder of the child and was still bound by the girdle.

Deprived of his splendor by the jewel, he was expelled from the camp. Indeed, for those who are mere Brahmins in name, this—shaving the head, confiscation of wealth, and expulsion from one's place—is the true execution; there is no other physical death for them.
Afflicted with grief for their sons, all the Pāṇḍavas, together with Kṛṣṇā,
performed the funeral rites for their deceased kin, beginning with the procession of the bodies.
Sūta said:
Then,
placing Kṛṣṇa at their head, the women went to the Gaṅgā to offer water for their deceased kinsmen who were longing for it.
Having all offered the water and lamented intensely once more, they returned.
Having bathed in the waters of the river purified by the dust of Hari’s lotus feet,
Mādhava [beheld] Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of the Kurus, seated there with his younger brothers, as well as Gāndhārī, afflicted by grief for her sons, Pṛthā, and Kṛṣṇā.
He consoled those whose kinsmen had been slain and who were overwhelmed with grief by means of the sages, demonstrating to all beings the course of time and the impossibility of retaliation;
he then recovered his own kingdom, which had been seized by gamblers from Ajātaśatru.
Having caused the death of that wicked king, whose life had been wounded by the touch of Kaca’s hair,
he performed for him three horse-sacrifices according to the most excellent ritual manuals; thereby,
he spread his purifying fame in all directions like that of Indra.
Having taken leave of the sons of Pāṇḍu, accompanied by Śaineya and Uddhava,
and having been honored in return by Dvaipāyana and other Brahmins who had honored him,
O Brāhmaṇa, he set his mind on departing for Dvārakā and mounted his chariot.
He perceived Uttarā running toward him, overwhelmed by fear.
Uttarā said:
"Save me, save me, O Great Yogi, God of gods, Lord of the Universe!"

"I see no other source of fear than you, O Lord, wherein death pursues one another. O All-pervading Master, let this arrow of heated iron burn me as it pleases; O Protector, let my fetus not be destroyed."
Sūta said:
Having understood her words, the Blessed One, who is compassionate toward his devotees,
realized that the weapon of Droṇa’s son was intended to render this world devoid of the Pāṇḍavas.
Then, O best of sages, seeing those five blazing arrows aimed directly at themselves, the Pāṇḍavas took up their own weapons,
perceiving that calamity facing them whose minds were fixed on no other object.
With his own weapon, the Sudarśana, the all-pervading Lord Hari— Himself the Self dwelling within all beings and the master of yoga— provided protection for His own people;
by means of His own māyā, He concealed the embryo of Vairāṭī for the sake of the lineage of the Kurus.
O descendant of Bhṛgu, although the Brahmāśiras weapon was unfailing and irresistible,
it was extinguished upon encountering the Vaiṣṇava splendor;
do not consider this a wonder, for in Acyuta, who is composed of all wonders, nothing is surprising.
The unborn one, who by means of the divine Māyā creates, protects, and destroys,
together with his sons who are devoid of Brahmanic splendor and with Kṛṣṇā—
unto Kṛṣṇa, who was facing his departure, the virtuous Pṛthā spoke this.
Kuntī said:
I bow down to You, the Primal Person, the Lord who is beyond material nature,
unperceivable by all living beings, and situated both within and without.
The imperishable Adhokṣaja, concealed by the curtain of *māyā*, is not perceived by those of ignorant vision, just as an actor wearing his costume is not recognized by those with deluded sight;
so too is he [unperceived] by the *paramahaṃsa* sages of pure soul.

For the purpose of prescribing the yoga of devotion, how indeed may we women behold Him? To Kṛṣṇa, to Vāsudeva, the son of Devakī, the youth of Nanda the cowherd, and Govinda— salutations, salutations!
Salutations to the one whose navel is a lotus; salutations to the one who wears a garland of lotuses; salutations to the one with lotus-eyes; salutations to You, whose feet are like lotuses.
O Hṛṣīkeśa, just as Devakī was imprisoned for a very long time by the wicked Kaṃsa and afflicted with grief...
O All-pervading Lord, I and my sons have been repeatedly liberated from a multitude of calamities by You alone, our Protector— from poison,
from the great fire, from the sight of man-eaters, from the assembly of the wicked, and from the hardships of dwelling in the forest;
and in every battle, O Hari, we have been protected from the weapons of many great chariot-warriors and even from the weapon of the son of Droṇa.
O Teacher of the World, may those calamities befall me perpetually here and there,
provided that they result in a vision of You, which is a vision beyond rebirth.
For a man whose pride increases through birth, sovereignty, learning, and prosperity—
Indeed, it is not even possible to describe You, who are the domain of those possessing nothing;

salutations to the one whose wealth is nothingness, whose activity regarding the qualities has ceased, who delights in the Self, who is peaceful, and who is the Lord of absolute liberation. Salutations!
I consider you to be Time, the Lord, without beginning or end,
the all-pervading one who moves equally toward all beings; yet no one understands Your purpose here, O Blessed One, as You enact this mockery of men through their mutual strife.
To him no one is ever dear and no one is ever hateful, yet men harbor a biased mind toward him;
O Soul of the Universe, that birth and action of the unborn, non-acting Self among animals,
humans, sages, and aquatic creatures is an absolute mockery.

O Gopī, while you stood there with your face cast down out of fear, your eyes agitated and blurred with tears as you held the rope upon me who had committed an offense— that very state of yours bewilders me, for even fear itself fears her.
Some say that the unborn Lord was born for the sake of the fame of Puṇyaśloka.
In the lineage of Yadu, who was as dear as sandalwood to Mount Malaya,
another [son] appeared through Devakī by the request of Vasudeva.
You, O Unborn One, have come for his protection and for the destruction of the enemies of the gods.
Others were born at the request of the Self-born (Brahmā) for the purpose of relieving the burden of the earth— which was sinking like a boat in the ocean due to its excessive weight—
in this world where beings are tormented by ignorance, desire, and karma.
Thinking, "I shall perform deeds worthy of being heard and remembered," some people constantly hear, sing, praise, remember, and rejoice in Your activities;
they alone, before long, behold Your lotus feet, which bring an end to the flow of worldly existence.
O Lord, have You perhaps today abandoned us because of our own past deeds— us, Your friends and dependents,
whose only refuge among kings afflicted by sin is Your lotus feet?
And what are we— the Pāṇḍavas together with the Yadus— other than mere names and forms?
O Wielder of the Mace, when there is no sight of you, as when there is no sight of the Lord of the senses, this place will no longer shine there as it does now,
marked by your footprints distinguished by their unique characteristics.
"These regions are flourishing, with their medicinal herbs and creepers fully ripened;
indeed, they prosper through your glances, O Lord of forests, mountains, rivers, and oceans.
Now, O Lord of all, Soul of all, whose form is the universe, [grant me] among your own people..."
"Sever this firm bond of affection for the Pāṇḍus and Vṛṣṇis;
O Lord of Madhu, let my mind, which has no other object than You, truly find delight in You alone,
just as the Ganges finds its current in the ocean."

O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, friend of Kṛṣṇa, bull among the Vṛṣṇis, destroyer of the enemies of Avidhṛt, whose prowess is inexhaustible and who consumes the lineages of the kṣatriyas; O Govinda, You who descend to remove the suffering of cows, brahmins, and gods; O Lord of Yoga, teacher of all, Blessed One, obeisances unto You!
Sūta said:

Thus praised with melodious words by Pṛthu, Vaikuṇṭha, whose every manifestation is complete, smiled gently as if bewildering her with his illusory power (māyā). Having addressed her with the words "So be it," he entered the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura).
And as he was about to depart for his own city, though he was entreated with affection by the king,
by Vyāsa and others who were commanded by the Lord, and even by Kṛṣṇa of wondrous deeds through ancient histories, he did not wake up, being overwhelmed by grief.

The king, the son of Dharma, reflecting upon the slaughter of his friends, spoke, O brahmins, having fallen under the sway of affection and delusion through his materialized self: "Alas! Behold the ignorance rooted in the heart of this evil-minded one!"
"Many akṣauhiṇīs of an alien body—
belonging to one who has betrayed children, the twice-born, friends, allies, fathers, brothers, and gurus—
have been slain by me; surely there shall be no liberation from hell for me, even after tens of thousands upon tens of thousands of years."

"The killing of enemies in a righteous war is no sin for a king who sustains his subjects"— this scriptural injunction does not convince my mind regarding this act of treachery that has arisen here against women whose kinsmen were slain by me.
I cannot be cleansed by domestic rituals performed as householders,
just as muddy water cannot be cleansed by mud or liquor by liquor; likewise, one cannot wipe away the singular sin of killing a living being through sacrifices.
Sūta said:
Thus, fearing the enmity of his subjects and desiring to know all duties,
he then went to Vinaśana, where Devavrata fell.

Then all those brothers, O brahmin sages, followed with chariots drawn by excellent horses adorned with gold; likewise Vyāsa, Dhaumya, and the others did so. The Blessed Lord as well, O brahmin sage, went by chariot together with Dhanañjaya.
The king shone with them like Kuvera with the Guhyakas;
seeing him fallen upon the earth like an immortal descended from heaven,
the Pāṇḍavas, along with their followers and the wielder of the discus (Kṛṣṇa), bowed down before Bhīṣma.
O best of men, all the Brahman-sages, celestial sages,
and royal sages were there to behold the bull among the Bharatas;
[there were] Parvata, Nārada, Dhaumya, and the venerable Bādarāyaṇa.
Bṛhadaśva, Bharadvāja with his disciples, the son of Reṇukā (Paraśurāma), Vasiṣṭha, Indrapramada, Trita, Gṛtsamada, Asita,
Kakṣīvat, Gautama, Atri, Kauśika, and Sudarśana;
O Brahmin, other stainless sages as well— Brahmarāta and others,
along with Kaśyapa, Aṅgiras, and the rest— arrived accompanied by their disciples.
Upon perceiving that those highly fortunate ones had assembled, the best of the Vasus [approached them].

Knowing the dharma and discerning the distinctions of place and time, he who understood Kṛṣṇa’s power worshiped him as he sat there; the knower of dharma worshiped the Lord of the Universe, who dwells within the heart, though his form had been assumed through *māyā*.
To the sons of Pāṇḍu, who were seated before him, joined by humility and affection, he spoke with eyes blinded by tears of love:
"Alas, what misery! Alas, what injustice, that you, the delights of Dharma, [should be in this state]!"
"You ought not to live a life of misery, having fallen away from the dharma of the brahmins and losing your refuge.
Now that the great chariot-warrior Pāṇḍu has passed away, his young widow Pṛthā,
who has children, has repeatedly endured many sufferings on your account."
I consider everything that is unpleasant to you to be brought about by Time;
for the world, along with its protectors, is under his control, like a row of clouds driven by the wind—
even where King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, and Vṛkodara, mace in hand, reside.

Kṛṣṇa is not a woman, and the Gāṇḍīva is a bow; Kṛṣṇa is his friend, and therefore there is no calamity. For never, O King, does any man know His purpose, for even the wise become bewildered when striving to understand it.
Therefore, O bull among the Bharatas, having determined that this world is governed by destiny,
O Lord, protector of the helpless, follow his will and protect your subjects.
For he is indeed the Blessed One himself, the primordial Person Nārāyaṇa.

Deluding the world with his illusory power (*māyā*), he moves incognito among the Vṛṣṇis. O King, the Blessed Lord Śiva knows his most secret majesty, as do the celestial sage Nārada and the Blessed Lord Kapila himself.
Him whom you consider your maternal cousin, your dear friend, and your best well-wisher— whom you made your minister, messenger, and charioteer out of friendship—
that [action] was not fitting for one who is the Self of all, who views all equally, who is non-dual, and free from egoism.
The mental discrepancy caused by that [birth] does not exist anywhere in Him who is beyond reproach;
nevertheless, behold His compassion toward those of exclusive devotion,
since Kṛṣṇa Himself has appeared before my very eyes as I am about to cast off my life-breaths.
The yogi who, having fixed his mind upon Him with devotion and chanting His name with his speech,
casts off the body, is liberated from the bonds of desire and karma.
May that God of gods, the Blessed Lord, wait until I have cast off this body.
With a serene smile and four arms, his lotus-face was radiant with reddish eyes that seemed to quiver; he stood within the range of meditation.
Sūta said:
Having heard this, Yudhiṣṭhira [beheld him] lying there within the cage of arrows.
While the sages were listening,
he inquired about the various duties ordained according to the nature of the person, according to caste (*varṇa*), and according to stage of life (*āśrama*),
as well as those characterized by both [worldly attachment and renunciation] through the limiting conditions of passion and dispassion, as they have been handed down in the scriptures.

O Sage, [you have described] the duties of charity, the duties of kings, and the duties pertaining to liberation in their respective divisions; the duties of women and the duties concerning the Blessed Lord, both in brief and in detail; and the goals of virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation, along with their means, exactly as they are.

The knower of reality described various narratives and histories as he was proclaiming the dharma; while he was speaking, that time arrived which is desired by yogis who have mastery over death— the northern solstice.

Then, having withdrawn his speech, the leader of thousands fixed his mind, freed from all attachment, upon Kṛṣṇa— the primordial Person standing before him with four arms and shimmering yellow garments— with eyes half-closed;
and by means of that pure concentration, his impurities destroyed, he was instantly relieved of the exhaustion caused by his weapons through the very sight of Him.
With the delusions of the functions of all his senses ceased, he offered praise to Janārdana while dismissing the bridegroom.
Śrī Bhīṣma said:
Thus was his mind fixed, free from thirst, upon the Blessed One, the Supreme Lord, the foremost of the Sātvatas, the All-pervading.

May there be for me faultless devotion toward my friend Vijaya, who— while the stream of worldly existence continues even as He has withdrawn His own bliss to sport somewhere in Prakṛti— bears a body the color of the tamāla tree, adorned with garments as white as sunbeams, and whose lotus-face is veiled by a mass of curling locks, and who is beloved by the three worlds.

May Kṛṣṇa, whose face was adorned with drops of perspiration stirred by his mane as he shook the dust of the horses' hooves in battle, and whose skin was being pierced by my sharpened arrows despite his shining armor— may He,
having heard the words of His friend, suddenly stationed His chariot between His own army and the enemy's.
May my devotion be unto Him, the friend of Arjuna, who, while standing there, took away the lives of the enemy soldiers with His very glance; and who,

seeing the front of the opposing army, perceived it as a fault because He was averse to the slaughter of His own kin, removed that evil-mindedness through the knowledge of the Self— may I have devotion at the feet of that Supreme One.

Abandoning his own scripture and having leaped down from his chariot to uphold my true promise, he— standing upon the wheel of that very chariot, with his heavy mace swinging and his upper garment disarrayed— rushed forward like Hari to slay an elephant.
Struck by my sharp arrows, his armor shattered and drenched in blood, he faced me as an assailant.
May that Blessed One Mukunda, who violently pursued him for the sake of my slaughter, be my refuge.

May there be devotion in me toward that Blessed One— who possesses a victorious chariot and family, who holds the whip and grasps the reins of the horses, and who is worthy of being beheld for his splendor— whom, when seen here, even those destined for death have returned to their true nature.

The cowherd women, their pride aroused by his graceful gait, charming smiles, and affectionate glances, became blinded by intoxication and imitated his every action; yet they eventually returned to their natural state within the assembly hall of King Yudhiṣṭhira’s Rājasūya sacrifice, which was crowded with hosts of sages and eminent kings.
Worthy of worship and worthy of being beheld, this Self has appeared within the range of my vision; I have attained Him,
the unborn, who dwells in the heart of every embodied being who imagines themselves as separate,
like the single sun appearing manifold as individual reflections, and I have thereby shaken off the delusion of duality.
Sūta said:
Thus, having absorbed his own self into the Supreme Lord, his very self, through the activities of mind, speech, and sight, he ceased breathing within.
Perceiving that Bhīṣma had attained absorption into the partless Brahman,
they all became silent, like birds at the end of the day;
there, the drums sounded, played by both gods and men.
The virtuous praised him, and showers of flowers fell from the sky for the kings. O descendant of Bhṛgu,
after Yudhiṣṭhira had caused the funeral rites and other ceremonies for the deceased to be performed, he remained sorrowful for a moment.
The sages, filled with joy, praised Kṛṣṇa with his secret names;
thereafter, their hearts fixed on Kṛṣṇa, they returned once more to their own hermitages.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, accompanied by Kṛṣṇa, went to Hastināpura.
He consoled his father and the ascetic Gāndhārī; then,
authorized by his father and approved by Vāsudeva,
the powerful king ruled the kingdom inherited from his father and grandfather according to dharma.
Śaunaka said:

Having slain his rivals for the inheritance—the murderous aggressors—in battle, Yudhiṣṭhira, the foremost among the upholders of dharma, was deprived of his food along with his younger brothers; how did he conduct himself thereafter, and what did he do?
Sūta said:

Having caused the lineage of Kuru, which had been consumed by the forest fire of the Kali age, to sprout anew, and having established Yudhiṣṭhira in his own kingdom, Hari, the Lord who brings about the welfare of the world, became truly pleased in mind.
Having heard what Bhīṣma had spoken and then what Acyuta had said, his delusions were shaken away by the dawning of realized knowledge;
like Indra, he who has no other refuge than the Unconquered ruled the earth bounded by the horizon, followed by his younger brothers.
The rain-cloud poured forth at will, and the earth yielded all desires.
The cows, their udders full, joyfully drenched the cow-pens with milk;
the rivers, oceans, mountains, along with the trees and creepers,
and all medicinal herbs, yielded fruit according to the season and his every desire.
Neither mental anxieties, nor physical ailments, nor afflictions caused by fate, spirits,
or the self ever arose for living beings while that king, Ajātaśatru, reigned.
After Hari had resided in Hastināpura for several months, [he departed].
For the sake of dispelling the grief of his friends and out of a desire to do what was pleasing to his sister,
he took leave of her; having been permitted by her, he embraced and saluted her,
and then, being himself embraced and saluted by some, he mounted the chariot.
Subhadrā, Draupadī, Kuntī, as well as the daughter of Virāṭa;
Gāndhārī and Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Yuyutsu, Gautama, and the twins; Vṛkodara, Dhaumya, and the women, including the daughters of the Matsya king and others.

Bewildered, they could not endure the separation from the wielder of the Śārṅga bow; yet even a wise man who has attained freedom from evil attachments through the company of the virtuous cannot bear to abandon Him,
for his fame, when being recounted, brings delight upon even a single hearing.

How could the sons of Pṛthā, who have fixed their minds upon Him, endure separation from Him— [separation] from whom they were never parted by seeing, touching, conversing, sharing a bed, a seat, or a meal?
All of them, with unblinking eyes, had their hearts drawn toward Him.
Gazing [at him], bound by affection, they wavered here and there; out of longing for the son of Devakī, they restrained their welling tears,
lest it be said by the women of the kinsmen that some misfortune had occurred as he departed from their home.
Mṛdaṅgas, conchs, kettledrums, lutes, small drums, and gomukhas,
as well as dhundhurīs, yānakas, bells, and other instruments, resounded like dundubhis;
and the Kuru women, having ascended the rooftops of the palaces, [gathered] out of a desire to see.

With eyes glancing with love, bashfulness, and smiles, they showered Kṛṣṇa with flowers. Guḍākeśa, the beloved of his dearest friend, took up a white umbrella adorned with strings of pearls and a handle of jewels.
Uddhava and Sātyaki fanned Him with two most wonderful whisks,
and the Lord of Spring shone upon the road as flowers were scattered over Him.
Here and there, truthful blessings uttered by the twice-born were heard.

Among those whose minds were fixed on the Lord of Excellent Renown, there arose mutual conversations— some appropriate and some not— with respect to the One who is beyond qualities yet whose nature consists of qualities;
these discussions captivated the hearts of all who heard them among the women of the Kuru king’s city.

Indeed, this ancient Person, who was alone in the beginning within the Self— indifferent to the modes of nature, the Lord of the world, with His senses closed and His potencies dormant as if asleep during the night— is now once again impelled by His own potency, desiring to create the material nature which is His own life-force and the source of illusion.

Desiring to bestow form and name upon the Self which is without name or form, the author of the scripture proceeded [to do so]. Indeed, that very state which the wise—whose senses are conquered and whose vital breath is subdued—behold with a stainless soul uplifted by devotion; surely this [scripture] is capable of wiping away all impurity.
He is indeed this one whose virtuous stories are sung by his friends in the Vedas and in secret scriptures by those who speak of the mysteries;
He is the one Lord who, through the play of His own nature, creates, maintains, and devours the universe, yet remains unattached therein.
For when kings live according to unrighteousness and their intellects are shrouded in darkness, it is said that He manifests there through the mode of goodness.
He bestows fortune, truth, cosmic order, compassion, and glory; for the sake of worldly existence, He assumes various forms age after age.
Oh, how sufficient is the most praiseworthy lineage of Yadu! Oh, how sufficient is the most meritorious forest of Madhu!
For this bull among men, the Lord of Śrī, honors them by His very birth and by His wandering through them.

Oh, how wonderful! Kuśasthalī surpasses all other regions in celestial glory and brings auspicious fame to the earth, for its inhabitants constantly behold their own Lord, who is moved by His grace, with His smiling glance.
Indeed, the Lord of the Day (the Sun) must surely have been worshipped through vows, ablutions, and oblations by those women who have taken His hand in marriage.

The women of Vraja, whose hearts were captivated by the hope of Him, repeatedly drank the nectar of His friendship; those who were won as brides by the price of His prowess at the *svayaṃvara* after He had crushed the powerful kings headed by Śiśupāla;
and others, such as Pradyumna, Sāmba, Amba, and their daughters, who were brought away by the thousands upon the slaying of Narakāsura.

"Alas! These women, though they have cast aside their natural delicacy and abandoned all purity, yet perform what is truly virtuous for the sake of womanhood—that from whose home the lotus-eyed husband never departs, touching their hearts with his embraces.
As the city women were speaking these words, [the Lord heard them].
Glancing back with a smile of welcome, Hari departed; meanwhile,
Ajātaśatru, fearing his enemies and out of affection for the protection of the Madhu-slayer, dispatched his fourfold army.
Then Śauri, having firmly turned back the Kauravas who had come from afar and were distressed by separation, departed for his own city with those dear to him—
[passing through] Kurujāṅgala, Pāñcāla, Śūrasena, and the lands along the Yamunā.

Having passed through Brahmāvarta, Kurukṣetra, the Matsyas, and the Sārasvatas, and then beyond Marudhanva, the powerful Bhārgava reached the Sauvīras and Ābhīras; his horses being somewhat fatigued, he arrived at the Ānartas.
In each place, Hari was met by the local inhabitants with offerings of hospitality;
then, having entered the cow-pen, he took his evening rest in the western direction as the sun had set.
Then Sūta said:
Having approached his own prosperous kingdom of Ānarta,
he blew his excellent conch shell as if to dispel the dejection of its people.
With its white belly and the deep red glow of the lower lip of the Wide-Striding Lord (Urukrama), that conch shone brilliantly even though it was a cave-like vessel.
Like a loud-sounding swan in a cluster of lotuses within a pair of hollowed hands, He blew His conch;
hearing that roar which brought terror to the world,
all living beings, longing for the sight of their Lord, came forward to meet Him.
There, having respectfully presented offerings to the Sun like lamps, they—
whose faces were blossoming with affection and whose voices were choked with joy— spoke to Him who delights in the Self, whose desires are eternally fulfilled by His own attainment.
Like children bowing to their father, who is the friend and protector of all,
we bow always to Your lotus feet, O Lord, which are worshiped by Viriñca, the sons of Viriñca, and the lords of the asuras;
You are the supreme refuge and the ultimate security for those desiring well-being in this world, where even Time, the supreme master, has no power.
O Creator of all beings, may you become our very existence; you alone are our mother, our friend, and our lord father.
You are our true guru and our supreme deity, by following whom we have become perfected.
Oh, how blessed we are to have you as our protector—you who are difficult even for the inhabitants of the three heavens to behold!
May we behold Your form, which possesses all auspiciousness and whose face is graced by affectionate smiles and loving glances.
O lotus-eyed One, when You depart for the Kurus or the Madhus out of a desire to see Your friends,
let even a single moment there be equal to ten million years for us, who are without You, O Acyuta— just as it would be for one deprived of the sun to his eyes.

"O Lord, how shall we live while you have been away for so long, not beholding your charming face adorned with a beautiful smile— that which dries up all suffering with its gracious glance? Thus addressed by the words of the people, he who is affectionate toward his devotees...
Hearing [the news] and extending his favor with a glance, he entered the city,
which was protected by the Madhus, Bhojas, Daśārhas, Ārhakas, Kukuras, Andhakas, and Vṛṣṇis—
men whose strength equaled his own— just as Bhogavatī is guarded by the Nāgas.

It possessed the beauty of lotus ponds surrounded by gardens, groves, and pleasure-grounds, featuring hermitages with trees and creepers that yield all seasons and all riches; its gateways, doors, and paths were adorned with festive arches.
The city had its heat warded off by the tops of variegated banners and flags;
its great highways, streets, marketplaces, and crossroads were thoroughly swept;
it was sprinkled with scented water and strewn with fruits, flowers, unbroken grains, and sprouts.

At every door of the houses, the high-minded Vasudeva heard that his dearest one was approaching— the doors adorned with curd, unbroken grains, fruits, sugarcane, full water-jars, offerings, incense, and lamps.
Akrūra, Ugrasena, and Rāma of wondrous prowess;
Pradyumna, Cārudeṣṇa, and Sāmba, the son of Jāmbavatī—
their beds, seats, and meals were all heightened by the force of their great joy.
