Placing the lordly elephant at their head, accompanied by Brahmins bearing auspicious items, and honored by the sounding of conchs and trumpets and the chanting of the Vedas,
they went out to meet him in their chariots, joyful yet overcome with affectionate trepidation.
And hundreds of courtesans, eager for the sight of him, arrived in vehicles,
their faces and cheeks radiant with the luster of shimmering earrings;
as did actors, dancers, Gandharvas, bards, panegyrists, and heralds.
And they sang of the wonderful deeds of the One of Excellent Renown.
There, the Blessed One approached his kinsmen and the citizens who followed him according to the prescribed rites, and he bestowed honor upon them all.
The Lord, having consoled those from the lowest castes with humble salutations, embraces, the touch of his hand, and smiling glances,
and having granted them their desired boons,
was himself attended by his elders, the Brahmins, together with their wives and the aged.
Accompanied by the blessings of others and by bards, he entered the city.
O Brahmin, when Kṛṣṇa had set out upon the royal road, the noble women of Dvārakā climbed to the rooftops of their mansions, for they were celebrating the great festival of beholding him.
Even for the inhabitants of Dvārakā who gaze upon him constantly,
their eyes are never satiated with Acyuta, the abode of Śrī and the very limb of her splendor;
he whose chest is the dwelling place of Śrī and whose face is the drinking vessel for the eyes.

The arms of the world-protectors served as his parasol and fly-whisks, while his lotus feet were honored by showers of flowers along the path; dressed in saffron robes and adorned with a forest garland, he shone like a rain-cloud accompanied by the sun, the moon, a rainbow, and lightning.
Having entered the home of his parents, he was embraced by his mothers;
with joy, he saluted the seven women headed by Devakī with his head bowed low.
They, their breasts overflowing with milk from maternal affection, took their son upon their laps.
Their souls overwhelmed with joy, they drenched him with tears from their eyes.
Then he entered his own abode, unsurpassed and fulfilling all desires,
wherein were palaces and sixteen thousand wives.
Seeing their husband returned home from his journey, the wives experienced a great festival of joy in their minds;

rising suddenly from their seats and beds even from a distance, they stood with their eyes and faces bashful due to their vows. With deep inner devotion, they embraced their husband with the very glances of their sons.
O best of the Bhṛgus, although the flow of tears was restrained by their shame before you, it overflowed from their eyes due to their agitation;
for even though he was at her side in private, she found his pair of feet ever new at every step— she who, though fickle, never leaves his feet, even when she is moving.

Thus, having incited enmity among kings whose splendor was encompassed by *akṣauhiṇī* armies— kings born as a burden upon the earth— he ceased from mutual slaughter like the wind ceasing a fire, and became disarmed;
it is he who has descended here into this world of men by his own *māyā*.
Seated upon the pinnacle of the jewels of women, the Blessed One took his pleasure like an ordinary man, he whose pure and lovely smiles revealed unrestrained passion,
and by whose bashful glances even the God of Love was struck down.
Having become utterly bewildered, she cast aside the bow shot by the most excellent of women—
He whose senses no deceptions were able to disturb;
yet this world considers Him, though detached, to be attached.

Because the ignorant person does not perceive the human being as himself through the analogy of his own self, he fails to recognize this lordship of the Lord; yet, though situated within material nature, he is not bound by its qualities, just as the intellect resting in the true Self is not affected, even while it depends upon that [nature].

Those foolish women, not knowing the true measure of their husband, thought him in private to be devoted only to women and under their influence, just as the intellects of those who do not know the Lord [perceive Him].
Śaunaka said:

The embryo of Uttarā was destroyed by the supreme splendor of the Brahma-head weapon unleashed by Aśvatthāman; it was restored to life again by the Lord. [I shall now describe] the birth and the deeds of that great-souled one of vast intelligence.
We wish to hear how his end came to pass and the manner in which he departed after death; please tell this to us who have faith, if you deem it fit to speak, for Śuka imparted this knowledge to us.
Sūta said:
Dharmarāja protected his subjects like a father,
pleasing them while remaining free from desire for all objects of enjoyment through his devoted service to the feet of Kṛṣṇa.

O twice-born ones, what use have you for those desires cherished by the gods— abundant wealth, sacrifices, celestial worlds, a queen, brothers, sovereignty over Jambūdvīpa, and fame that has reached the third heaven— if your minds are fixed on Mukunda?
They brought joy to the king, just as others might to one who is hungry; at that time,
O descendant of Bhrigu, the hero while still within his mother’s womb beheld a certain person being scorched by the splendor of a weapon.

He is the size of a thumb, stainless, wearing a shimmering golden crown; He is of dark complexion with a most beautiful appearance, clothed in lightning, the infallible Acyuta, possessing four long arms adorned with splendid earrings of refined gold.
With bloodshot eyes and mace in hand, he was wandering in every direction; like Indra with his thunderbolt, he repeatedly brandished his mace, which shone like a meteor,
extinguishing the splendor of the enemy's weapons as mist with a cloud.
As he was dispersing [the demons] nearby, [the sage] looked around, wondering, "Who is this?
Then the immeasurable Self, the Lord Hari, the all-pervading protector of dharma,
vanished right there while the ten-month-old child was looking on.
Then, when all the qualities were at their peak and the planets had risen favorably,
there was born to Pāṇḍu a son who would uphold his lineage, possessing strength like another Pāṇḍu.
With a joyful heart, the king, together with the brahmins headed by Dhaumya and Kṛpa, [performed the rites].
Having had the birth ceremony performed and the auspicious recitations chanted,
that king, who was conversant with sacred rites, bestowed gold, cows, land, villages, and excellent elephants and horses upon the Brahmins at the *prajā-tīrtha*, and gave them abundant food.
The brāhmaṇas, being satisfied, spoke with humility to the king:
"O bull among the Pauravas, since this lineage of Puru has come to an end through the irresistible power of fate while [the king] was still in his youth," [they said].
Out of favor toward you, he was bestowed by the all-powerful Viṣṇu;
therefore, he will be known in the world by the name Viṣṇurāta— of this there is no doubt, O highly fortunate one, for he is a great devotee of the Lord.
The King said:
O best of beings, did these great-souled royal sages of virtuous fame follow after his glory and his reputation for goodness?
The brāhmaṇas said:
O son of Pṛthā, you are a protector of subjects in person, like Ikṣvāku, the son of Manu;
you are devoted to the brāhmaṇas and true to your promise, just like Rāma, the son of Daśaratha.
He is a giver and a refuge, just like Śibi, the son of Uśīnara; he will spread the fame of his own people, like the son of Duṣyanta among the performers of sacrifice;
he is the foremost of archers, equal to both Arjunas.
He is as unassailable as fire, as difficult to cross as the ocean,
as valiant as the king of beasts, and as worthy of service as the Himalayas; he is patient like the earth, enduring like the parents, and forbearing like the earth itself.
In equanimity he was equal to his grandfather [Brahmā], and in graciousness he was like Giriśa [Śiva]; he was the refuge of all beings, just as the Lord is the refuge of Ramā;
in the greatness of all his excellent qualities, he was devoted to Kṛṣṇa.
Magnanimous like Rantideva, righteous like Yayāti, equal to Bali in his devotion to Kṛṣṇa, and possessing noble resolve like Prahlāda,
he is a performer of horse sacrifices and a devoted attendant upon the elders.
He is the progenitor and instructor of royal sages, the subduer of those who wander onto the wrong path, and the restrainer of the Kali age for the sake of dharma on earth;
he shall meet his death at the hands of Takṣaka, dispatched by the son of a twice-born.
Having heard this, he will attain the state of Hari, freed from all attachments; and having sought the true nature of the Self from the sage who is the son of Vyāsa,
O King, he will truly depart for that place which is free from fear, leaving this world behind in the Gaṅgā.
Having thus instructed the king, all those brahmins, experts in the science of birth-rites,
having received their due honors, returned to their own homes.
This very lord is renowned in the world as Parīkṣit.
Reflecting upon what he had seen before, he would examine the men here on earth.
That prince grew quickly, like the bright moon in its waxing phase,
being filled day by day by his ancestors as the moon is filled by the lunar phases.
Desiring to perform the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) with the intent of expiating his offense against his kinsmen,
the king, having acquired wealth, reflected that there was no means other than taxes and fines.
Perceiving his intention, his brothers were impelled by Acyuta.
They brought back vast amounts of lost wealth from the northern direction;
with those resources fully gathered, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma,
being apprehensive, worshipped Hari with three horse-sacrifices.
Summoned by the king, the Blessed One, having performed the sacrifice for the monarch with the assistance of the twice-born,
dwelt there for several months out of a desire to please his friends.
Then, permitted by the king, he departed together with Kṛṣṇā and his kinsmen.
O Brahmin, accompanied by Arjuna and surrounded by the Yadus, he went to Dvāravatī.
Sūta said:
On his pilgrimage, Vidura learned from Maitreya the destiny of his own soul.
Having learned this, he went to Hastināpura with her, having attained his desire for knowledge;
and after the steward (Kṣattṛ) had asked as many questions as he did before Kauṣārava, he developed singular devotion to Govinda and desisted from those [other inquiries].
O Brahmin, seeing that kinsman arrived, Dharmaputra (Yudhiṣṭhira) along with his younger brothers,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Yuyutsu, the Sūta (Saṃjaya), Śāradvata (Kṛpa), Pṛthā,
Gāndhārī, Draupadī, Subhadrā, Uttarā, and Kṛpī [all went out to meet him].
Other female relatives of Pāṇḍu, as well as his kinsmen along with their wives and sons,
went out to meet him with great joy, like the vital breath returning to the body; they approached him according to custom, embracing him and offering salutations.
Distraught by the longing of separation, they shed a flood of tears of love.
The king honored him once he had accepted a seat;
when he had eaten, rested, and was seated comfortably upon his throne, [the king approached].
Bowing down with humility while they were listening, King Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Do you perhaps remember us, who were nourished by the shade of your wings?"

By what means of livelihood did you sustain yourselves while wandering over the circle of the earth, you who, together with your mother, were delivered from a multitude of calamities such as poison and fire,
and who have served sacred fords and the foremost of holy places here on this earth?
O Lord, devotees like you, who are yourselves sacred pilgrimage sites,
sanctify other holy places by virtue of the Wielder of the Mace residing within your hearts.
O dear one, even we are your friends and kinsmen, for Kṛṣṇa is our supreme deity.
"Have you seen or heard anything of the Yadavas, who dwell happily in their own city?
Thus addressed by Dharmarāja, he described all of that in sequence exactly as it had been experienced, omitting only the destruction of the Yadu clan.

Indeed, though it was unpleasant and difficult for men to endure, He— being compassionate and unable to bear seeing them in distress— did not inform them that [the enemy] had arrived of His own accord. Then, honored like a god, He dwelt there happily for some time.
Doing what was beneficial for his eldest brother and bringing happiness to all, he acted as the restrainer (Aryaman),
duly inflicting punishment upon those who committed sins;
thus Yama maintained his status as a Śūdra for a hundred years due to the curse.
Yudhiṣṭhira, having regained his kingdom and seeing his grandson— the upholder of the lineage—
along with his brothers who were like world-protectors, rejoiced in supreme splendor.
Thus, for those attached to their homes and distracted by the activities of worldly life...
The supremely insurmountable time, remaining unrecognized, has passed away. Having understood this, Vidura spoke to Dhṛtarāṣṭra:
"O King, depart quickly; behold, this danger has arrived."
O Lord, he for whom there is no remedy from anyone at any time—
this very Blessed Time has arrived for all of us,
by whom we are overtaken even though life is most dear to us.
A person would be separated from them instantly; how much more so from other things such as wealth?
Your father, brothers, friends, and sons have been killed;
your own youth has passed away, and you, seized by old age, now dwell in the house of another.
Formerly blind and now deaf, with failing intellect,
with broken teeth and weak digestion, full of lust and vomiting phlegm—
oh, how great is a living being's hope for life, as seen in you!
He eats the morsel offered by Bhīma like a domestic dog.
Fire has been unleashed, poison has been administered, and wives have been defiled;
for those whose fields and wealth have been stolen, what is the use of the lives they give?
Even this body of yours, wretched and desiring to live,
will depart against your will, worn out by old age like two garments. Detached and freed from bonds, one should abandon this body once its purpose has been fulfilled.
He whose course is unknown to others is indeed called wise.

He who, having become detached from this world— whether through his own efforts or those of others— and possessing self-mastery, places Hari within his heart and departs from his home, is the best of men.
"Now, may you go toward the northern direction, your course unknown even to yourself;
for from this point on, time will generally draw away the qualities of men.
Thus was the King of the Ajamīḍha lineage, whose eye was his wisdom, enlightened by his younger brother Vidura.
Having severed the bonds of affection for his own kin, he departed with firm resolve along the path shown by his brother.
As her husband set out, the virtuous and devoted wife, the daughter of Subala, followed him;
she was like the joyful encounter of the staff-bearing sage Nyasta-daṇḍa with Himālaya, or like the battle of the high-minded heroes.

Having performed his duties of friendship and offered oblations into the fire, Ajātaśatru bowed to the brahmins and, having honored them with sesame seeds, cows, land, and gold, entered his home to pay respects to his elders; however, he did not see his parents or the daughter of Subala.
There, with an anxious mind, he questioned Sañjaya, who was seated there.
"O son of Gavalgaṇa, where is our father, aged and blind?
And where is our mother, afflicted by the loss of her sons? Where has our uncle, our dear friend, gone—he who, though I am of unrefined intellect, was deprived of his kinsmen along with his wife?"
Hoping to wash away his impurity, he fell into the Gaṅgā in distress.
Now that our father Pāṇḍu has passed away, where have our two paternal uncles gone, who protected all of us children— our friends— from calamity?
Sūta said:
Out of compassion and due to the agitation caused by his affection, Sūta was emaciated by separation;
failing to see the Lord of his soul, he was so deeply afflicted that he could not respond.
Wiping away his tears with both hands and steadying himself by his own effort,
he spoke to Ajātaśatru while remembering the feet of the Lord.
Sañjaya said:

"O delighter of the family, I did not know the resolve of my parents, nor that of Gāndhārī, O mighty-armed one; I have been robbed by these great-souled ones. Then the blessed Nārada arrived together with Tumburu.
Rising up and greeting the sage with his younger brothers, Yudhiṣṭhira honored him and said:
"O Blessed One, I do not know the destination of my parents; where have they gone from here?"
"Or is it my mother, distressed by the loss of her son? Where has that poor woman gone?
Then the Blessed One, Nārada, the best of sages, spoke like a helmsman who shows the shore to those in the boundless ocean.
Nārada said:
O King, do not grieve over anything, for the world is under the control of the Lord;
these worlds, along with their guardians, bring tribute to that Ruler.
He alone unites living beings, and He alone separates them;
just as oxen are tied by their noses to a rope and bound with cords,
so too are they bound by names to the rope of speech and carry tribute to the Lord.
Just as in this world the union and separation of the toys used for play occur by the will of the player, so too do they occur for human beings by the will of the Lord.
As for whether you consider the world to be permanent, impermanent, or neither—

In every respect, they are not to be lamented, except for the grief born of delusion arising from affection. Therefore, my dear friend, abandon this despondency of yours caused by ignorance; how indeed will those wretched ones live without me, left as they are without a protector?
This body, composed of the five elements, is subject to time, karma, and the modes of nature;
how can it protect others, just as one seized by a serpent cannot protect another?
Those without hands are protected by those with hands, and those without feet by those with four feet.
In this world, all things are insignificant; the living soul is the life of the living, and the life of that soul is the Lord.
O King, behold Him—the one Blessed Lord, the self-effulgent witness of all selves—who shines as both the inner and the outer, yet remains concealed by His own illusory power.
O Great King, this very Lord,
the creator of all beings, has now descended in this world in the form of Time for the destruction of the enemies of the gods;
his divine task having been accomplished, he awaits only the remainder.
"Watch over them until the Lord Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
together with his brother and his wife Gāndhārī,
has gone to the hermitage of the sages south of the Himālayas."
The celestial river (Svardhunī), which indeed divided itself into seven streams,
is called "Seven-streamed" (Saptasrotas) because it was manifested in various ways for the pleasure of the seven [sages].
Having bathed therein at each of the three daily libations and having offered oblations into the fires according to the prescribed rule, [he performed his rites].
Subsisting on water alone, his mind tranquil and free from all desires,
he sat with his posture conquered, his breath controlled, and his six senses withdrawn;
by meditating upon Hari, the impurities of the qualities of passion (rajas), goodness (sattva), and ignorance (tamas) were destroyed.
Having joined [the self] with the conscious self (vijñānātman), and having dissolved that [conscious self] into the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña),
one should place the self within Brahman, the substratum, like the space within a jar [is placed] in the [great] sky.
With the manifestations of the qualities of Māyā destroyed and the senses and the internal organ restrained, [one remains].
Having desisted from all food, he sat motionless like a pillar.
Do not create an obstacle for him, who has renounced all ritual actions.
O King, on the fifth day from today, he—either he himself or another—will [attain his goal].
He will cast off his body, and that body shall be reduced to ashes.
While the husband’s body is being consumed by fires within the hut,
the virtuous wife, standing outside, will follow her husband into that fire.

O descendant of Kuru, Vidura, having witnessed that marvel, was filled with both joy and sorrow; departing from there, he became a seeker of sacred fords (tīrtha). Having spoken thus, Nārada then ascended to heaven along with Tumburu.
Yudhiṣṭhira, taking his words to heart, abandoned his sorrows.
Sūta said:
When Arjuna had set out for Dvārakā, desiring to see his kinsmen...
And while some months had passed since Arjuna had departed from there to learn of the deeds of the virtuous Kṛṣṇa,
that best of the Kurus beheld omens of a terrible nature.
He saw the terrible course of time, in which the seasons have their properties inverted;
the wretched livelihood of men whose souls are consumed by anger, greed, and falsehood; and social dealings that are mostly crooked, as well as friendships mixed with deceit.
When the time had arrived for men, there appeared signs of extreme calamity, such as the mutual malice of fathers, mothers, friends, brothers,
and couples; seeing that the nature of unrighteousness, beginning with greed, had taken hold, the king spoke to his younger brother.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Jiṣṇu was dispatched to Dvārakā out of a desire to see his kinsmen and to learn of the activities of the virtuous Kṛṣṇa.
"Seven months have now passed, O Bhīmasena; your younger brother does not come.
For what reason? I do not know this clearly.
Yet, as instructed by the celestial sage, this very time has arrived."
When the Blessed One desires to cast off that limb of His which is His playground,
from which our prosperity, kingdom, wives, life-breaths, family, progeny,
victory over enemies, and the celestial worlds have arisen through His grace— [that very limb He now casts off].
"Behold, O tiger among men, the portents— celestial, terrestrial, and atmospheric—
that foretell a terrible danger not far off which will delude our minds. My thighs, chest, and arms, my dear, throb again and again."
And there is a trembling in my heart; they will soon do me an injury. This auspicious one with a face like fire is howling at the rising sun, and this dog is barking at me like a coward, O dear one.
The sacrificial animals turn me to the left, while others turn to the right;
O tiger among men, I perceive even my draft-animals weeping.
This dove is a messenger of death, and this owl makes my heart tremble.
Owing to the hooting of owls facing the new moon, they indeed perceived the entire universe as empty;
the quarters were smoky, the horizons were ablaze, and the earth along with its mountains trembled, O dear one, accompanied by great atmospheric crashes and thunderclaps.
The wind blows with a harsh touch, scattering the dust of *rajas* and the darkness of *tamas*;
the clouds rain down blood as if from all sides in a loathsome manner.
Behold the sun, its luster destroyed, and the mutual conflict of the planets in the sky.
With the two worlds, heaven and earth, as if set ablaze by swarms of agitated elemental beings, the rivers, streams, lakes, and even the minds of men were all thrown into turmoil.
Fire does not burn with clarified butter; what will this Time (Kāla) do?
The calves do not suckle at the udders, nor do the mothers yield milk;
the cows, with tearful faces, low in distress, and the bulls in the pen are no longer joyful.
The deities seem to weep, perspire, and tremble.
"These districts, villages, cities, gardens, mines, and hermitages—
bereft of their splendor and devoid of joy, why do they present such an evil sight to us?
I think that by these great portents, the footprints of the Blessed One have surely been erased."

O Brahmana, while the king was thinking, "The earth has been robbed of its great fortune by women who possess the beauty of no other man," the ape-bannered Arjuna returned from the city of the Yadus with a mind that perceived ill omens.

Seeing his younger brother fallen at his feet— uncharacteristically distressed, with his face cast downward and shedding teardrops from his lotus-eyes— the king’s heart was filled with anxiety upon beholding him so pale.
Remembering what had been spoken by Nārada, he questioned [his grandfather] in the midst of his friends.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Are our own kinsmen living happily in the city of Ānarta?"
O venerable one, is all well with the Madhus, Bhojas, Daśārhas, Ārhas, Sātvatas, Andhakas, and Vṛṣṇis? Is Śūra, your maternal grandfather, well?
And is your maternal uncle Ānakadundubhi, along with his younger brothers, in good health?
His seven sisters— his wives, maternal aunts, and their daughters— along with their daughters-in-law,
headed by Devakī, are themselves dwelling there in safety. I hope King Ahuka is alive, as is his sonless younger brother.
Is Hṛdīka well, along with his son Akrūra, and Jayanta, Gada, and Sāraṇa? Are those led by Śatrujit and the others also doing well?
And does the blessed Rāma, the lord of the Sātvatas, abide in happiness?
The great chariot-warrior Pradyumna dwells in happiness among all the Vṛṣṇis; and the blessed Aniruddha, possessing profound speed, is indeed flourishing,
as are Suṣeṇa, Cārudeṣṇa, and Sāmba, the son of Jāmbavatī.
And others who were preeminent among the followers of Kṛṣṇa, such as Ṛṣabha and his sons;
likewise the attendants of Śauri, such as Śrutadeva, Uddhava, and others;
and those other bulls among the Sātvatas, headed by Sunanda and Nanda.
Are they all living in well-being, sheltered by the arms of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa?
Do they, bound by their affection, still remember our welfare?
And is the Blessed Lord Govinda, who is devoted to the brāhmaṇas and compassionate toward his devotees, also well?
I hope he dwells happily in the Sudharmā assembly hall, surrounded by his friends;
for the auspiciousness, the welfare, and the prosperity of the worlds,
does that primordial Person, the friend of Ananta, remain within the ocean of the Yadu clan?
In his city, which is protected by the staff-like arms of the Lord, the Yadavas—
those of great prowess— sport in supreme bliss like honored kings;
and by the primary act of serving His feet, Satyabhāmā and the other sixteen thousand women [attain their goal].

Having conquered the gods in battle, the heroic Yadus— who live by the power of his staff-like arms and are fearless from any quarter— frequently seize with their feet the Sudharmā assembly hall, which is fit for the best of the gods and was brought there by force, even though it is the object of the gods' blessings and appropriate for the wielder of the thunderbolt.

"O dear one, I hope you are free from ailment; you appear to me as if your splendor has faded. Have you been treated with contempt because you failed to obtain [what you sought], or have you been away for a long time, my son?
I hope you have not been struck down by inauspicious things, such as unpleasant sounds and other sense-objects."

Have you not given what was promised to those who asked with hope? O giver of refuge, have you ever abandoned a Brahmin, a child, a cow, an elderly person, a sick person, a woman, or any living being who has come to you for protection?
I hope you have not approached a woman who should not be approached, or one who is unchaste, or one who has not been honored; nor have you been defeated on the road by those superior or equal to you?
And have you perhaps eaten before you had fed the elderly and the children?
Have you not committed any despicable act that was unworthy?
Or perhaps, because you are constantly separated from your dearest friend—the very core of your heart—you feel empty; otherwise, such pain would not be yours.
Sūta said:
Thus Kṛṣṇa, the friend of Kṛṣṇa (Viṣṇu), was questioned by his brother, the king; emaciated by separation from Kṛṣṇa (Viṣṇu), he assumed a form that was a source of various doubts.
With his lotus-like face and heart withered by grief and his luster lost,
he was unable to respond while remembering only that all-pervading Lord. With great difficulty, he steadied himself against his sorrow and wiped his eyes with his hand.
Distressed by the intense longing of his love for Him who was out of sight,
and recollecting their friendship, kindness, and affection during their times as charioteers and so forth,
he addressed the King, his elder brother, with a voice faltering with tears.
Arjuna said:
"O Great King, I have been deceived by Hari in the form of a kinsman;
by him my great splendor, which causes wonder even to the gods, has been taken away from me."
Indeed, through separation from Him for even a moment, the world becomes unpleasant to behold;
for, deprived of His hymn of praise (*uktha*), this world is said to be like a corpse.
Through taking refuge in Him, the kings who had come to the site of the *svayaṃvara*—intoxicated by the god of love at its commencement—[found relief].
Indeed, his splendor was taken away by me and the fish was struck down with my strung bow; Kṛṣṇā was won back in his presence;

and having swiftly conquered Indra along with the hosts of gods, I gave the Khaṇḍava forest to Agni. Having obtained the assembly hall fashioned by me through wonderful craftsmanship and magic, the kings brought tribute from all directions for that sacrifice.
O King, your noble younger brother, who possessed the strength and valor of ten thousand elephants, struck down the kings with his splendor for the sake of the sacrifice;
those kings were brought by him for the sacrifice of the Lord of the Pramathas, and because they were liberated by him, he presented them as an offering at your ritual.
Furthermore, O Lord, while your wife was preparing for the great consecration of the sacrifice, her most praiseworthy and beautiful hair was seized by gamblers in the assembly hall.

He whom his wives—whose faces were bathed in tears, whose hair was disheveled, and who had abandoned their ornaments upon seeing the slain body—touched as they fell at his feet after scattering [the remains]; he who, having come to the forest, protected us from the unbearable hardship inflicted by Durvāsas, the consumer of ten thousand offerings;
and he by whom the three worlds were considered satisfied when, submerged in water with his entire host, he partook of the remnants of a meal of vegetables.
Then, by his splendor, the Lord who bears the trident along with the daughter of the mountain was struck with wonder in battle and gave me his own weapon;
and other gods as well, through this very body, granted me half of the great throne in the abode of Mahendra.
While I was sporting there, the gods bestowed upon me a pair of staff-like arms marked by the *gāṇḍīva* bow for the sake of slaying my enemies.

O descendant of Ajamīḍha, I have been robbed today by that Supreme Person, the Infinite, whose power even Indra and the other gods depend upon. That my kinsman, alone on a chariot, crossed the ocean of the Kuru army—

boundless and impossible for others to cross— and that I recovered much wealth from the enemies and seized from their heads the jewel-studded crest-ornaments which were the very seat of their splendor.

O Lord, he who was the vanguard of the leaders of my chariot-divisions— that one who, with his mere glance, robbed of life, mind, and vital energy the vast armies of Bhīṣma, Karṇa, Droṇa, Śalya, and other preeminent kings adorned with circles of excellent chariots; and he upon whose arms were placed [the weapons] by the venerable Bhīṣma, Karṇa, the grandson of Droṇa, Trigarta, Śalya, the King of Sindhu, Bāhlīka, and others.
The weapons of the demons, whose power was unfailing, did not touch me, the servant of Nṛhari, just as they had failed before;
for the Lord, the Master of my soul, was chosen by me at the Sautya sacrifice despite my evil mind—He whose lotus feet the fortunate worship for liberation from worldly existence.
When I stood upon the ground, the chariot-warriors, though their horses were exhausted, did not strike me, for their minds were cast away by the majesty of His power.

O King, the playful jests of Mādhava— adorned with noble and beautiful smiles, addressed as "O Pārtha," "O Arjuna," or "O friend, joy of the Kurus"— which were so heart-touching that they used to roll within my heart; and how, through our oneness in lying, sitting, walking, joking, eating, and other activities, I was deceived by Him who said, "I am truthful."
Like a friend to a friend, like a father to his son, that Great One, by virtue of His majesty, endured all the wickedness of my foolish mind.

O King of men, now that I am bereft of that Supreme Person—my dear friend, my well-wisher, and my very heart—I am as if empty; while protecting the followers of the Wide-Strider on the path, O dear one, I have been utterly defeated by these wretched cowherds, like a weak woman.
"That bow was mine, those were my arrows, that was my chariot, those were my horses, and I myself was the charioteer, O kings, before whom you all bowed down.
All of that, in an instant, became as non-existent as an offering poured into ashes or seed sown upon barren soil, for it was devoid of the Lord.
"O King, thus have we, your friends, described our own friends in this city of ours, as you requested."
Deluded by the curse of the brahmins and striking one another with their fists,
their minds agitated by intoxication after drinking the wine of Varuṇa,
they were reduced to four or five survivors, as if they did not even recognize each other.
Generally, this is the activity of the Lord, the Sovereign:
that beings kill one another and nourish one another,
just as in the water the larger aquatic creatures devour the smaller.
O King, the strong overpower the weak, and the great overpower other strong ones;
in this same way, the powerful Yadus, being great, caused the others to subdue one another, and thus the Lord brought about the removal of the earth's burden through the Yadus themselves.
"The words spoken by Govinda, which are appropriate to place and time and which pacify the distress of the heart, steal away the mind of one who remembers them.
Sūta said:
As Jiṣṇu was thus contemplating the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa,
his pure intellect became tranquil through an exceedingly deep affection,
its momentum increased by the constant meditation upon the feet of Vāsudeva.
Arjuna, whose intellect had its entire impurity scrubbed away by devotion,
the Lord, having once again attained that knowledge sung by the Blessed One on the front lines of battle— which had been obstructed by time, karma, and darkness— became empowered once more.
Free from sorrow through the attainment of Brahman, with all doubts regarding duality severed,
he was beyond rebirth because his material nature had dissolved, being devoid of the three modes and lacking any material designation;
thus he heard the path of the Blessed One and the final state of the Yadu dynasty.
With his mind composed, Yudhiṣṭhira set his heart on the path to heaven;
and Pṛthā, having heard from Dhanañjaya both the destruction of the Yadus and that departure of the Blessed One,
fixed her soul with exclusive devotion upon the Lord Adhokṣaja and ceased from the cycle of worldly existence.
The unborn Lord abandoned that body by which he had removed the burden of the earth;
for the Lord, both [the body and its abandonment] are equal, just as one thorn is removed by another thorn.
Just as he assumes forms such as the Fish and others, so too does he abandon them like an actor.

When the Blessed Lord Mukunda, whose virtuous deeds are worthy of being heard, cast off this earth along with his own body— having thus exhausted the burden of the world— he abandoned that physical form.
At that very moment, Kali, the cause of misfortune for those of unawakened minds, set in.

The wise Yudhiṣṭhira, having reflected upon that creeping wheel of unrighteousness— consisting of greed, falsehood, crookedness, violence, and so forth— which pervades the city, the kingdom, the home, and likewise the self, resolved to depart. He,
the sovereign, [entrusted] his own grandson, who was disciplined and equal to himself in virtues, [with the kingdom].
In Gajāhvaya (Hastināpura), he consecrated Toyanīvi as the lord of the earth;
likewise, in Mathurā, he then consecrated Vajra as the lord of Śūrasena.
Having performed the Prājāpatya sacrifice, the Lord then absorbed the sacrificial fires within himself.
Having cast aside there all those things, such as his silken garments and bracelets,
free from possessiveness and egoism, with all bonds completely severed,
he offered his speech into the mind, and the other senses into that breath.
In death he offered the drinking-vessel along with its contents; for when it reached the state of fivefold dissolution, the sage called out to it.
Having offered the state of three into the state of five, he then offered that into the state of one. He offered everything into the Self, and the immutable Self into Brahman.
Clad in rags, abstaining from food, with speech restrained and hair disheveled,
he displayed his own form like one who is dull-witted, insane, or a ghost; looking about without regard for others, he went forth as if deaf, not hearing a thing.
He entered the northern direction, previously traversed by the great-souled ones,
meditating in his heart upon the Supreme Brahman, from which, once gone, one does not return.
All his brothers, having made a firm resolve, followed after him.
Seeing that the people on earth had been touched by Kali, the friend of unrighteousness,
those who had accomplished all their goals through virtuous deeds recognized this as the ultimate state for themselves and mentally took refuge in the lotus feet of Vaikuṇṭha.
Those supreme ones, whose intellects were purified by devotion intensified through meditation upon Him,
attained that state of Nārāyaṇa which is the goal of single-minded intent— a goal difficult to reach for those who are wicked and whose souls are absorbed in sense-objects.

With their impurities shaken off, they indeed went to that place by means of their own stainless selves; Vidura also, having abandoned his body at Prabhāsa with his mind absorbed in Kṛṣṇa, went to his own abode along with his ancestors.
And Draupadī, perceiving that indifference of her husbands toward worldly concerns,
attained single-minded devotion to the Blessed Vāsudeva. Whoever with faith hears this account of the departure of the sons of Pāṇḍu, who were beloved by the Blessed One, [attains the same].
Having heard this supreme, auspicious, and purifying account, one attains devotion to Hari and achieves perfection.
Sūta said:
Thereafter, the great devotee Parīkṣit ruled the earth according to the instruction of the best of the twice-born.
O Brahmin, just as those expert in the science of procreation had predicted regarding his great qualities, so it was;
he married Irāvatī, the daughter of Uttara,
and through her he begot four sons, Janamejaya and the others.
He performed three horse-sacrifices at the Gaṅgā with abundant sacrificial fees,
having appointed Śāradvata as his priest, wherein the gods became visible to his eyes.
In one instance during his world-conquest, that hero forcibly subdued Kali by his own prowess.
Śaunaka said: Why did the king seize Kali during his world conquest while he was killing a cow couple with his foot, though wearing the marks of a king?
"O Śūdra, who is this man bearing the marks of a human and a god who struck the cow with his foot? O highly fortunate one, let that be told if it concerns the stories of Kṛṣṇa;
or rather, if it concerns the holy men who lick the nectar of his lotus feet."
"What is the use of other worthless talk, which is but a waste of life? O dear one, for mortals of short lifespan who desire the eternal truth,
the Blessed Lord Death has been summoned here for the ritual of the sacrificial slaughter."
No one dies here as long as the Ender (Antaka) remains present;
for this very purpose, the Blessed One was invoked by the supreme sages.
Oh! In the world of men, may the nectar-like words describing the pastimes of Hari be drunk!
For one who is dull, of dull intellect, and indeed of dull lifespan,
the night is stolen away by sleep and the day by futile activities.
Sūta said:
When Parīkṣit, residing in Kurujāṅgala, heard the unpleasant news that Kali had entered his own sovereign realm, he, being skilled in battle, took up his bow and mounted his chariot—
which was well-adorned, yoked with dark horses, and bore the banner of the lion— departing from the city.
Surrounded by his own army consisting of chariots, horses, elephants, and infantry, he set out for the conquest of the quarters; having conquered Bhadrāśva, Ketumāla, Bhārata, the Northern Kurus,
Kimpuruṣa, and the other regions, he received tribute from them.
Dhanañjaya beheld cities and forests, rivers of pure water, men resembling gods, and women of lovely appearance— all of whom he had never seen before and who were full of auspicious beauty.
He beheld splendid dwellings and women resembling apsarases; there, in various places, he heard the glory of his own great-souled ancestors being sung, proclaiming the majesty of Kṛṣṇa.
Having saved himself from the power of Aśvatthāman’s weapon,
and seeing the affection of the Vṛṣṇis and Pārthas for them, as well as their devotion to Keśava,
he was supremely satisfied with them, his eyes overflowing with joy.
The high-minded one gave them costly garments and necklaces; [he offered] the roles of charioteer, attendant, servant, friend, and messenger,
as well as the honors of sitting with him as an equal, following him, praising him, and prostrating before him.
The king offered his prostrations to Viṣṇu, who is affectionate toward the Pāṇḍus,
and he practiced devotion at the lotus feet of that very Lord.
As he was thus conducting himself daily, following the conduct of his ancestors, [the Lord appeared].
Not far from there, indeed, was a marvel that occurred; listen to it from me.
Dharma, walking on a single foot, perceived a cow that had lost its luster and asked her—she who resembled a mother whose calf had been taken away—with tears upon her face.
Dharma said:
"O blessed lady, is there no ill-health for you? You appear lusterless, with a somewhat withered face.
I perceive that you have internal distress; O mother, you are grieving for some relative far away."

Do you grieve because you yourself are deprived of one foot, or because you will be eaten by outcasts; or rather, do you grieve for the gods and others who have been robbed of their sacrificial shares, or for the subjects when Indra fails to send rain?
Or do you grieve, O Earth, for women and children left unprotected, as if they were tormented by man-eaters?

The goddess of speech [is degraded] in families of Brahmins who perform unrighteous acts and lack Vedic knowledge; the foremost of the lineage are [degraded] in royal families consisting of mere kṣatriba-bandhus afflicted by the Kali age; and the kingdoms are overthrown by them, while the world of living beings is intent on eating, drinking, clothing, bathing, and sexual intercourse here and there.

Or rather, O Mother Earth, tell me this root of your anxiety, by which you are so distressed— why you, though released from your burden, still remember the deeds of Hari, the bearer of the earth, who has now withdrawn his incarnation and whose activities have been suspended until final liberation.
"Or has your fortune, honored by the gods, been taken away by Time, the strongest of the strong, O Mother?
The Earth said:
"You indeed know all that you ask me concerning dharma."
By means of four feet that bring happiness to the world, You abide;
these are truth, purity, compassion, forbearance, renunciation, contentment, straightforwardness,
tranquility, self-control, austerity, equanimity, endurance, detachment, and sacred learning.
Knowledge, detachment, sovereignty, heroism, splendor, strength, memory,
independence, skill, beauty, fortitude, gentleness,
boldness, humility, character, endurance, vitality, power, and fortune.
Profundity, steadfastness, faith, fame, self-respect, and freedom from egoism—
these and other great qualities, O Blessed One, are eternally present in him;
they are sought by those desiring greatness and never depart from him at any time.
Therefore, now that I am deprived of that vessel of virtues, the abode of Śrī, I grieve for this world beheld by the sinful Kali age,
and I also mourn for myself and for you, O best of immortals.
The gods, ancestors, seers, virtuous men, and all the social classes as well as the stages of life—
beginning with Brahmā— having taken refuge in the Blessed One, have repeatedly performed austerities, desiring liberation through the glance from His corner of the eye.

She is Śrī, who, having abandoned her own dwelling, the forest of lotuses, is devotedly attached to the auspiciousness of his feet; of him, whose banners are marked with the lotus, the thunderbolt, the goad, and the banner... [I am the servant].
Her body adorned by the glorious footprints of the Blessed One,
she outshone the three worlds upon perceiving that splendor; then, at its conclusion, he released me as I was smiling.
He who, being self-reliant, indeed dispelled the hundred akṣauhiṇīs— the excessive burden of the kings of the Asura lineage—
and by his own prowess placed you, who were in a precarious and inferior position, within himself.
While bestowing his beautiful form upon the Yadus,
who could endure separation from the Supreme Person, with His loving glances, radiant smiles, and charming speech?

While the Earth and Dharma were thus conversing, the thrill of horripilation that arose within me at the sight of her feet stole away the composure of those women who prided themselves on their sweetness.
The royal sage named Parīkṣit reached the eastern Sarasvatī.
Sūta said:
There, the king saw a pair of cows being slaughtered like those who have no protector.
And he saw the low-born man, bearing the insignia of royalty, with a staff in his hand;
he was like a white lotus-stalk bull, appearing as if urinating while terrified,
trembling, reeling on one foot, and struck by a Śūdra.

Mounted upon his chariot adorned with gold, he questioned the cow— who was the yielder of dharma, yet now miserable, severely struck by the feet of a Śūdra, deprived of her calf, tearful-faced, emaciated, and longing for grass.
With a voice as deep as a rain-cloud, having strung his bow, he said:
"Who are you, a powerful man who by force violates the weak women in my domain?
You are a king in appearance, yet like an actor, you are a brahmin in deed."
O Kṛṣṇa, you who have gone far away with the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow—
you, who deserve compassion, yet strike down those unworthy of pity in secret, deserve death.
Or rather, you who are as white as a lotus stalk, though lacking feet, yet move about on your own feet.
Is some god, perhaps in the form of a bull, causing us distress?
For never upon this earth, which is embraced by the staff-like arms of the lords of the Kauravas, do the sorrows of living beings descend except for you.
"O daughter of Surabhi, do not grieve here; let your fear of the outcaste depart.
Do not weep, O Ambā; may it be well with you, for I am the punisher of the wicked. In whose kingdom all subjects tremble before the virtuous and the unrighteous..."
The fame, lifespan, fortune, and destination of that intoxicated man shall perish.
For this is the supreme duty of kings: the suppression of those who cause distress to others. Therefore, I shall slay him, the most wretched of men, who harms living beings.
"O four-footed bull, who cut off your three legs?
May there be no such as you in the kingdom of kings who follow Kṛṣṇa. Speak, O bull; may it be well with you; [you have harmed] the virtuous who have committed no offense."
"He who causes deformity to the self, who defiles the fame of the sons of Pṛthā,
and who inflicts sin upon innocent people— by subduing such a wicked man, there shall be well-being for the virtuous on all sides, and fear of me shall prevail."
"Against those beings here who are innocent, he who acts as an offender without restraint—
him I shall seize by the arm, even if he be an immortal, along with his bracelets. For the supreme duty of a king is indeed the protection of those established in their own duties."
While he was instructing others here on this earth— provided they were not in times of distress— to follow the path rather than the wrong way according to the scriptures,
Dharma spoke:
"O sons of Pāṇḍu, these words of yours, which grant fearlessness to the distressed, are indeed appropriate."

O bull among men, we do not recognize that Supreme Person, for we are deluded by the distinctions of words; yet it is by His multitude of virtues that the Blessed Lord was made their messenger and so forth— He from whom these seeds of suffering would otherwise arise.
Some, clothed in the veil of conceptual construction, say that the self is the cause of the self;
others say it is destiny, others action, and others the primal nature or the Lord. Some maintain the conviction that it is the inconceivable and indefinable.
"O royal sage, reflect upon this with your own intellect to find what is appropriate here.
Sūta said:
"O best of the twice-born, while he was thus proclaiming the dharma, that sovereign monarch—"
With a concentrated mind and free from weariness, he gazed upon him.
The King said:
"O knower of dharma, you speak of dharma; you are dharma itself, assuming the form of a bull."
Whatever place belongs to one who performs unrighteous acts shall also belong to the informer;
or rather, it is certain that the course of the divine māyā is beyond the reach of both the minds and the speech of living beings.
In the Kṛta age, austerity, purity, compassion, and truth were established as its four feet;
now, O Dharma, three of your feet have been broken by the portions of unrighteousness— namely, pride, attachment, and intoxication—
so that only your foot of truth remains to sustain you.
This Kali age, nourished by untruth, desires to seize him;
and this earth, burdened by her great weight, has been relieved by the Blessed One,
who has adorned her everywhere with His glorious footprints.
"The virtuous woman, like an unfortunate widow abandoned by her husband, shall weep with a stream of tears, thinking: 'These unrighteous men in the guise of kings—mere Śūdras—will devour me.
Having thus consoled both Dharma and the Earth, the great chariot-warrior [departed].
He drew his sharpened sword for the purpose of slaying me, who was the cause of unrighteousness;
perceiving him as one intent on killing, he cast off his royal insignia and,
overwhelmed by fear, fell with his head at the base of my feet.
The hero, compassionate toward the distressed, the protector, and the one worthy of praise, did not slay him as he fell at his feet; instead, smiling as it were, he spoke these words.
The King said:
"O Guḍākeśa, you who possess the splendor of Yaśodharā, there is no fear whatsoever for you who stand with palms joined in reverence.
You must not dwell in any way upon my field, for you are a kinsman of unrighteousness. As you exist within the bodies of gods among men, this multitude of unrighteousness has followed after you."
Greed, falsehood, theft, ignobility, sin, preeminent deceit, strife, and hypocrisy—

these bonds of unrighteousness must not be pursued; rather, one should live by righteousness and truth in Brahmāvarta, where those who understand the ritual expansions of sacrifice worship the Lord of Sacrifice with sacrifices.
In whom the Blessed Lord Hari, the very embodiment of sacrifice, being worshipped, bestows auspiciousness upon those who perform sacrifices;
he fulfills the unerring desires of all moving and stationary beings, like the vital air (vāyu) that exists both within and without them.
Sūta said:
Thus instructed by Parīkṣit, Kali, his body trembling with fear,
spoke this to him as he stood with sword raised like the wielder of the staff of punishment:
Kali said:
"O Universal Monarch, wherever I may dwell by your command,
there I shall perceive you holding your bow and arrows;
therefore, O best among the upholders of dharma, you should point out a place for me."
"Wherever I may dwell, I shall abide by your instruction.
Sūta said:
"Thus entreated, he then granted places for him to dwell."
Gambling, drinking, women, and the slaughterhouse—wherein fourfold unrighteousness resides.
Furthermore, the Lord gave gold to one who was begging;
from that arose falsehood, intoxication, lust, passion, and fifthly, enmity.
These five places were indeed granted by the son of Uttara; Kali, who originates from unrighteousness, dwelt there acting according to his instructions.
Therefore, a man desiring prosperity should never resort to these at any time.
In particular, the king, who was devoted to righteousness, the lord of the world, and the preceptor,
restored the three lost feet of Dharma— namely austerity, purity, and compassion—
and having comforted the earth, caused it to flourish once more.
He, that very king, now occupies this seat worthy of a monarch,
which was offered by his grandfather, the king, as he desired to enter the forest;
that royal sage now sits there, radiant with the splendor of the lord of the Kauravas.
O highly fortunate one, this king, the son of Abhimanyu, who rules in the city called Gajāhvaya, is a great emperor of vast renown and possesses such power as this;
while he protects the earth, you have been initiated for the sacrificial session.
Sūta said:
He who, though scorched by the weapon of Aśvatthāman’s son, did not die in his mother’s womb,
was saved by the grace of the Lord Kṛṣṇa of wondrous deeds.

He whose mind was dedicated to the Blessed Lord did not lose consciousness despite the loss of life caused by Takṣaka, which arose from the anger of Brahmā; for he had abandoned all attachment and understood the state of the Unconquered.

The disciple of Vyāsa’s son cast off his own body in the Gaṅgā; yet for those who relish the news of the Lord of Excellent Renown and who remember His lotus feet, there can be no agitation even at the time of death, as they partake of the nectar of His stories.
Even though Kali had entered everywhere here,
he could not prevail for as long as the great Lord remained on earth as the sole sovereign of the son of Abhimanyu.
On the very day that the Blessed One released the earth [from his hold]...
At that very time, Kali, who originates from unrighteousness, followed after him here;
yet the emperor did not feel aversion toward Kali, just as a bee, seeking only the essence, does not resent the flower.
For his auspicious deeds quickly reached fulfillment, while other actions performed did not.
What indeed has been gained by the hero Kali, who is wise yet fearless, against those who are childish?
He dwells among men like a wolf among those who are heedless while he himself is vigilant.
This meritorious account concerning the son of Parīkṣit has thus been described to you by me.
The narrative concerning Vāsudeva which you have requested—

whatever stories there may be of the Blessed One, whose great deeds are to be told, and which take His qualities and actions as their subject, those are to be cultivated by men who desire spiritual well-being.
The sages said:
O gentle Sūta, may you live for eternal ages and enjoy pure fame,
for you proclaim to us mortals the nectar of Kṛṣṇa’s deeds.
O Govinda, in this world of action which offers no security, you cause those whose nature is as soot-blackened by smoke to drink the honey-nectar from the lotus feet of the Lord.
We do not value even a fraction of heaven or liberation from rebirth as much as that.

What need is there to mention the blessings for mortals who associate with those who associate with the Blessed One? Who indeed could ever be satiated by the nectar of the narrations concerning Him who is the sole refuge of the Greatest Being?
Even the masters of yoga, headed by Brahmā and the lords of the worlds, did not reach the end of the qualities of that One who is beyond all qualities.

Therefore, O learned one, may you— who are preeminent among the Blessed Ones and whose sole refuge is the Great One— expound for us, who desire to hear it, the noble and pure life-story of Hari, the supreme devotee of the Great One. Indeed,
that Parīkṣit was a great devotee of the Lord, possessed of vast intelligence, by whom [the truth] known as liberation was attained.
Through the knowledge designated as "of Vyāsa's son," he took refuge at the feet of Him whose banner bears the king of birds.
Therefore, relate to us that supreme, meritorious narrative of unhidden meaning, which is grounded in most wonderful yoga,
endowed with the infinite deeds [of the Lord], concerning the son of Parīkṣit, and which delights the devotees of the Blessed One.
Sūta said:
"Oh, today we have truly borne fruit, even though born from a degraded womb, by following the elders!
The association with the names of the Great Ones quickly shakes off the wretchedness of one's lineage and mental anguish."
How much more so for one who chants His names, being solely devoted to Him, the Supreme among the Great?
He is the Blessed Lord of infinite power, whom they call Ananta because of His infinite qualities.
Indeed, is it not enough to have merely indicated this much, regarding His qualities which are without equal and unsurpassed?
The divine power attends upon him who does not even desire it, yet who abandons all other objects of pursuit;

moreover, the water released from the tips of his toenails—which Brahmā offers as a respectful offering—purifies the entire world along with Śiva himself. Who indeed in this world is a true possessor of lordly power (*bhagavat*) other than Mukunda?

In that [state] where the wise, being deeply attached, suddenly cast off their attachment to the body and so forth, they attain that final stage of the paramahaṃsas, in which non-violence and tranquility are one's own duty. For I have been asked by you, O Aryamanas; tell me here as much as there is of the realization of the Self.
Just as birds fly through the sky according to their own capacity, so too do the wise attain the goal of Viṣṇu according to their respective levels.
Once, while wandering in the forest on a hunt with his bow raised,
he pursued deer until he was utterly exhausted, hungry, and parched with thirst.
Not seeing the reservoir of water, he entered that hermitage;
there he saw the sage seated, peaceful, with eyes closed, having restrained his senses, vital breaths, mind, and intellect, and withdrawn from all activity.
Having attained the state beyond the three worlds, become one with Brahman, and free from all transformation—
though his matted locks were disheveled and covered by a deer skin,
and his parched throat longed for water— he begged for such sustenance.
Having received neither grass nor ground, and having obtained neither the respectful offering (*arghya*) nor kind words,
he felt as if he were being treated with contempt; and his soul,
already afflicted by hunger and thirst, suddenly became enraged at this unprecedented turn of events.
O Brahman, envy and anger arose toward the brāhmaṇa. In his rage, he placed a lifeless serpent upon the shoulder of the brahmin seer and,
departing with the tip of his bow, returned to his city.

"Is this one with all his senses withdrawn and eyes closed practicing a false meditation, or could he perhaps be a mere kṣatriya? His son, however, is exceedingly radiant as he plays with the other children."
Hearing that his father had been made to suffer this misfortune by the king, he spoke these words there:
"Alas! What unrighteousness on the part of protectors who are as fat as vultures! That servants, like dogs, should incur the sin of their master because of gatekeepers!"
"For the Brahmins have appointed a mere kṣatriya as the guardian of their household;
how can he, acting as a doorkeeper in that house, be worthy to eat from their vessels?
Now that the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, the teacher of those who have gone astray, has departed,"
"Today I shall punish those who have broken its embankments; behold my power!
Having spoken thus, the young sage, his eyes copper-red with rage, touched the waters of the Kauśikī and discharged the thunderbolt of his speech.
"Thus, on the seventh day, Takṣaka shall bite this one who has transgressed the bounds of propriety,
this charcoal of his lineage, as he is incited by me for his offense against my son. Then,
having returned to the hermitage, the boy found the carcass of a snake around his neck.
Seeing his father, he, afflicted with grief, wept aloud with a released throat. O Brahmin, that son of Aṅgiras, having heard the lamentation of his son,
slowly opened his eyes and saw the dead serpent upon his shoulder.
Having dismissed him, he asked, "Child, why indeed do you weep?
Or by whom has an offense been committed against you? Thus addressed, he reported [the matter].
Having heard that the king had been cursed for something he did not deserve, that brāhmaṇa did not congratulate his son.
"Alas! Oh, what a great sin you have committed today; for a very slight offense, you have imposed severe punishment.
O one of immature intellect, you ought not to measure the God of Men (Naradeva), who is known as the Supreme, by ordinary human standards.
Protected by His unbearable splendor, the subjects find auspiciousness and remain free from fear from any quarter."

"O dear one, while the Discus-bearer— whose name is the God of Men— is no longer visible, this world will then perish in an instant, overrun by thieves and left unprotected like a city without its ramparts. Therefore, a calamity that is beyond remedy now falls upon us, as the protector of our wealth has perished at the hands of a plunderer."
Then, like many plunderers, people will kill one another, curse one another, and seize the cattle, women, and wealth of others.
At that time, the noble dharma of men—consisting of the three Vedas and joined with the conduct of the social classes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*)—will dissolve away.
Consequently, for those whose minds are obsessed with material gain and sensual pleasure, there will be a confusion of castes, like that of dogs and monkeys.
He is a protector of dharma, a lord of men, a sovereign emperor of great renown;
he is a manifest and most fortunate royal sage who has performed the horse sacrifice.
Though he is distressed by hunger, thirst, and fatigue, he does not deserve our curse.
Whatever evil has been committed by me, a fool of immature intellect, against my own innocent servants, may the Blessed Lord, the Soul of all, forgive that.
Even those who have been insulted, deceived, cursed, reviled, or struck— [may He forgive them].

"Even though they are his powerful devotees, they do not offer him any remedy for that," [he thought]. Thus, the great sage, tormented by the sin committed against his son and personally mistreated by the king, did not dwell upon that evil at all.
Generally, in this world, when saintly persons are joined by others in pairs of opposites,
they neither feel distressed nor rejoice, because the self is the refuge beyond the modes of nature.
Sūta said:
Then the lord of the earth, reflecting upon that censurable deed committed by himself, became deeply dejected:

"Alas! I have acted baselessly like an ignoble man toward this innocent Brahmin of hidden splendor. Surely, because of my insult to the gods, a calamity difficult to overcome will befall me before long."
Let that indeed be sufficient as atonement for my sin, so that I may truly never act in such a way again.
May the fire of the Brahmana family, provoked by me, burn today itself my kingdom, my army, and my prosperous treasury—
the ill fortune of one like me— so that a mind more wicked than this toward the twice-born, the gods, and the cows shall never arise in me again.

While he was reflecting thus, he heard how the son of the sage had spoken of Nirṛti, known as Takṣaka. He considered it well that Takṣaka would soon become the cause of detachment for Nala, who was so deeply attached to worldly life.
Then, having previously reflected upon this world and the next as things to be abandoned, he prepared to leave them both behind.
Regarding the service of Kṛṣṇa’s feet as his highest goal, he sat down to fast unto death on the immortal river (the Gaṅgā).

Indeed, who that is about to die would not serve that river, which carries waters superior even to the dust of Kṛṣṇa’s feet mixed with shimmering Śrītulasī, and which purifies the worlds on both banks along with their lords?

Having thus resolved, that son of Pāṇḍu, with single-minded devotion, observing the vow of a sage and having abandoned all attachments, sat down to fast unto death on the banks of the Viṣṇupadī, fixing his mind upon the feet of Mukunda.
There, sages of great majesty accompanied by their disciples arrived, purifying the world.
Generally, by the pretext of visiting sacred fords (*tīrtha*), the virtuous themselves purify those very fords.
Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Cyavana, Śaradvān, Ariṣṭanemi, Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras,
Parāśara, the son of Gādhi (Viśvāmitra), Rāma, Utathya, Indrapramada, and Idhmavāha— [these sages visited the holy places].
Medhātithi, Devala, Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, Bhāradvāja, Gautama, Pippalāda,
Maitreya, Aurva, Kavaṣa, Kumbhayoni, the venerable Dvaipāyana, and Nārada;
as well as other eminent celestial sages, brahminical sages, and royal sages, such as Aruṇa and others.
Having honored those who had assembled there, belonging to various *ṛṣi* lineages and *pravara* clans, the king bowed his head to them.
Then, when they were seated comfortably, he again offered salutations and,
with a pure mind, standing before them with palms joined in reverence, informed them of what he intended to do.
The King said:

"Oh, we are most fortunate! Our character is such that we are worthy of being favored by the greatest of kings. Alas, the lineage of kings has been cast far away from the purifying touch of the Brahmins' feet due to our contemptible deeds."

For me, whose mind is constantly attached to household life, let the Brahmins and the divine Gaṅgā accept me as I approach Him— the Lord of the high and the low— who, appearing as the curse of the twice-born, is rooted in world-weariness and swiftly brings fear to one who is addicted to it, yet whose heart is fixed on the Supreme Lord.
May a snake sent by a twice-born man, or a fraudulent *takṣaka*, bite me sufficiently; sing the songs of Viṣṇu!

May there again be delight in the infinite Blessed One and association with the great ones who take refuge in Him. In whatever creation I enter, may there be friendliness toward all; salutations to the twice-born!

Thus resolved, the wise king sat upon *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing eastward on the southern bank of the ocean’s consort, facing north, having entrusted the burden of his kingdom to his son. While that god among kings remained thus seated in the vow of fasting unto death (*prāyopaveśa*), the hosts of gods in heaven—
Having praised him, they scattered flowers upon the ground; with joy, the kettledrums resounded repeatedly.

The great sages who had assembled there, praising and applauding with cries of "Excellent!", spoke words whose essence was compassion for all beings, concerning the virtues of the Lord of Excellent Renown (Uttaṃśloka).
"O best of royal sages, this is not surprising among you who have taken refuge in Kṛṣṇa—
those who, desiring the presence of the Blessed One, immediately abandoned their thrones adorned with royal crowns.
As for us, we shall all remain here until he has cast off this body."
"This foremost devotee shall go to the supreme world, which is free from passion and devoid of sorrow.

Having heard those words of the host of sages— which were consistent, sweet, weighty, and truthful— Parīkṣit greeted them with praise and, desiring to hear the deeds of Viṣṇu, spoke to them appropriately.
All of you have gathered here from every direction, like all the Vedas personified on this triple-peaked mountain.
Here, neither in this world nor in the next, is there any purpose whatsoever except for the supreme service of others, which is one's own true nature.
Therefore, O Brahmins, I ask you this which ought to be asked; please grant me your confidence in this matter.
While those who were dying were reflecting with their whole being upon what is pure and necessary to be done therein, the Blessed One, the son of Vyāsa— wandering the earth at will, indifferent,
his outward marks unrecognizable, content with his own gain, and dressed as an avadhūta surrounded by children— appeared there.
He was sixteen years of age, with delicate feet, thighs, arms, shoulders, cheeks, and limbs;

his eyes were beautiful and long, his nose prominent, his ears symmetrical, and his face graced by lovely eyebrows; his neck was well-formed like a conch shell, his collarbones were hidden, his chest broad and high, his navel spiraled, and his belly possessed folds and a beautiful waist.
Clad in the directions as their only garment, with hair disheveled over his face, long-armed, and possessing the splendor of the foremost of the gods;
dark-complexioned, yet eternally endowed with the beauty of limbs in the fullness of youth, and enchanting to women with his lovely smile—
those sages, though they were experts in the marks of such a person, rose from their seats before him who was of hidden majesty.
That Viṣṇu-rāta, for the guest who had arrived, bowed his head and offered him worship. Then, after the women, children, and others had withdrawn, he sat upon a great throne, having been honored.
There he was surrounded by hosts of the most exalted ones—the assemblies of Brahman-sages, royal sages, and celestial sages.
The Blessed Lord shone exceedingly, like the moon surrounded by a multitude of planets, constellations,
and stars. Approaching the sage of unimpeded intelligence as he sat in tranquility,
the devotee of the Lord bowed his head, stood with palms joined in reverence, and having prostrated, questioned him with truthful and pleasant words.
Parīkṣit said:

"O brāhmaṇa, oh! Today we, who are but wretched members of the kṣatriya order, have become worthy of being served by the virtuous, for you, by your very grace, have made us like sacred pilgrimage sites through your presence as our guests."
By the mere remembrance of them, the homes of men are indeed instantly purified;
how much more so by seeing them, touching them, washing their feet, or sharing a seat?
O Great Yogi, through their very presence, even the greatest sins [are destroyed].
They perish instantly for men, just as the enemies of the gods perished before Viṣṇu.
Is the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, who is dear to the sons of Pāṇḍu and a kinsman to that lineage, pleased with me out of affection for his father’s sister?
Otherwise, how could we mortals perceive You, whose movement is unmanifest—
especially those of us who are dying, when You are so perfectly accomplished and most venerable? Therefore, I ask about the perfection of yogis, O supreme teacher.
O Lord, please tell me what must be done by a person here in this world when dying in every way; what is to be heard, what is to be chanted, and what is to be performed by men;
or what is to be remembered or worshipped, or even the opposite thereof.
"O Brahmin, it is certain that even the time for milking the cows is never observed anywhere in the homes of householders belonging to the Blessed One.
Sūta said:
Thus addressed and questioned by the king with gentle words,
the venerable Bādarāyaṇi, who knows the dharma, replied.
